knowledge_statements.title: Reduced-Length Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records telescoping, nonnegativity, and tight-arc properties of reduced lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph, let \(\ell:A\to\mathbb R\), and let \(\pi:V\to\mathbb R\). Define
\[\ell_\pi(u,v)=\ell(u,v)+\pi(u)-\pi(v)\qquad((u,v)\in A).\]
For every directed path \(P\) from \(x\in V\) to \(y\in V\),
\[\ell_\pi(P)=\ell(P)+\pi(x)-\pi(y).\]
Thus reduced lengths preserve the ordering of paths with the same endpoints, and \(\pi(v)-\pi(u)\le\ell(u,v)\) for every \((u,v)\in A\) exactly when \(\ell_\pi(u,v)\ge0\) for every \((u,v)\in A\). If \(s\in V\), every vertex is reachable from \(s\), and \(\pi(v)=d_s(v)\) for all \(v\in V\), then every arc of any shortest-path arborescence rooted at \(s\) has reduced length zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reduced lengths telescope along paths, preserve comparisons between paths with fixed endpoints, are nonnegative exactly for feasible potentials, and vanish on shortest-path-tree arcs under distance potentials.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every directed \(x\)-to-\(y\) path \(P\), \(\ell_\pi(P)=\ell(P)+\pi(x)-\pi(y)\), and potential feasibility is equivalent to \(\ell_\pi(a)\ge0\) for every \(a\in A\).

notation.meaning: length function reduced by potential pi

knowledge_statements.title: Potential–Length Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes shortest-path length as the greatest feasible potential difference.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph with \(\ell:A\to\mathbb R\), let \(s,t\in V\), suppose that \(t\) is reachable from \(s\), and assume that \(G\) has no negative directed cycle. Then
\[d_s(t)=\max\left\{\pi(t)-\pi(s):\pi:V\to\mathbb R,\ \pi(v)-\pi(u)\le\ell(u,v)\text{ for every }(u,v)\in A\right\}.\]
The maximum is attained. For an attaining potential \(\pi\), define \(\ell_\pi(u,v)=\ell(u,v)+\pi(u)-\pi(v)\). A directed \(s\)-to-\(t\) path is shortest if and only if every one of its arcs has zero reduced length under \(\pi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The shortest source-target path length equals the maximum feasible potential difference, and under an attaining potential the shortest paths are exactly the paths composed of zero-reduced-length arcs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_s(t)=\max\{\pi(t)-\pi(s):\pi(v)-\pi(u)\le\ell(u,v)\ \text{for every }(u,v)\in A\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directed Shortest-Path Potential Duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Min-max equality for a reachable ordered vertex pair in a nonnegatively weighted digraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $D$ be a digraph with $\phi:E(D)\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq0}$, and let $u,v\in V(D)$ such that a directed $u$-$v$ path exists. Then
\[
\min_{P:u\leadsto v}\sum_{e\in P}\phi(e)=\max_{\substack{\pi:V(D)\to\mathbb{R}\\ \pi(y)-\pi(x)\leq\phi(xy)\ \forall xy\in E(D)}}\bigl(\pi(v)-\pi(u)\bigr).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If v is reachable from u in a nonnegatively weighted digraph, the shortest directed u-v path length equals the largest feasible potential difference from u to v.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{P:u\leadsto v}\phi(P)=\max_{\pi:\,\pi(y)-\pi(x)\leq\phi(xy)\ \forall xy\in E(D)}\bigl(\pi(v)-\pi(u)\bigr)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Shortest-path distance as a maximum potential difference
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Potential representation of an \(s\)-to-\(t\) distance using inequalities on arcs traversed by at least one \(s\)-to-\(t\) walk.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a digraph, \(s,t\in V\), and \(l:A\to\mathbb{R}\). knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The shortest-path distance from s to t is the maximum potential difference p(t)−p(s), subject to the potential inequality on every arc used by at least one s-to-t walk. For integral lengths, integral potentials suffice.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Max-Potential Min-Path-Length Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shortest-path duality through feasible vertex potentials, with the reachability boundary and integral-length consequence made explicit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a digraph, let \(r,s\in V\) be distinct, and let \(l:A\to\mathbb{Q}_+\). If an \((r,s)\)-dipath exists, then \[\max\{\phi(s)-\phi(r):\phi:V\to\mathbb{Q},\ \phi(v)-\phi(u)\le l(a)\ \forall a=(u,v)\in A\}=\min\{l(P):P\text{ is an }(r,s)\text{-dipath}\}.\] If every arc length is integral, an integral optimal potential exists. If no \((r,s)\)-dipath exists, the potential maximization is unbounded above.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When s is reachable from r, the largest feasible potential difference equals the length of a shortest directed r-to-s path. Integral arc lengths admit an integral optimal potential. Without an r-to-s path, the potential objective is unbounded.
assumptions_latex: \text{An }(r,s)\text{-dipath exists for the finite min--max equality}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max_{\phi(v)-\phi(u)\le l(a)}\bigl(\phi(s)-\phi(r)\bigr)=\min_{P:r\leadsto s}l(P),\qquad l\in\mathbb{Z}_+^A\Rightarrow\exists\phi^*\in\mathbb{Z}^V

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any weighted digraph $(D,\phi)$, there exists a map $\pi:V(D)\to\mathbb{R}$ satisfying $\pi(y)-\pi(x)\leq\phi(xy)$ for every arc $xy\in E(D)$ if and only if $D$ contains no directed cycle of negative total weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weighted digraph admits a feasible potential exactly when it contains no negative-weight directed cycle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(\exists\pi:V(D)\to\mathbb{R}\ \forall xy\in E(D),\ \pi(y)-\pi(x)\leq\phi(xy)\bigr)\Longleftrightarrow\nexists C\text{ directed cycle with }\sum_{e\in C}\phi(e)<0

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Min-Potential Max-Work Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Potential formulation of maximum directed-path length in an acyclic digraph, including integer attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be an acyclic digraph, let \(r,s\in V\) be distinct, and let \(l:A\to\mathbb Q_+\). Then the minimum of \(\phi(s)-\phi(r)\) over potentials \(\phi\) satisfying \(\phi(v)-\phi(u)\ge l(a)\) for every arc \(a=(u,v)\) equals the maximum \(l\)-length of an \((r,s)\)-dipath. If \(l\) is integer-valued, an integer-valued optimum potential exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an acyclic digraph, the minimum feasible potential difference from r to s equals the maximum length of an r–s directed path; integer arc lengths admit an integer optimum potential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{\phi}\{\phi(s)-\phi(r):\phi(v)-\phi(u)\ge l(a)\ \forall a=(u,v)\in A\}=\max\left\{\sum_{a\in P}l(a):P\text{ is an }(r,s)\text{-dipath}\right\},\quad l(A)\subseteq\mathbb Z\Rightarrow\exists\phi^*\in\mathbb Z^V\text{ optimal}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reduced Costs and Feasible Potentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines potential-based arc reweighting for a real-weighted digraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a digraph, \(c:E(G)\to\mathbb{R}\), and \(\pi:V(G)\to\mathbb{R}\). For each arc \((x,y)\in E(G)\), define its reduced cost by \(c_\pi(x,y):=c(x,y)+\pi(x)-\pi(y)\). The potential \(\pi\) is feasible when \(c_\pi(e)\ge 0\) for every \(e\in E(G)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An arc's reduced cost is its original cost plus the tail potential minus the head potential. A potential is feasible when all reduced arc costs are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: c_\pi(x,y)=c(x,y)+\pi(x)-\pi(y),\qquad \pi\text{ is feasible}\iff (\forall e\in E(G))\;c_\pi(e)\ge 0

knowledge_statements.title: Shortest-Path Tree Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certifies all single-source distances using tight tree arcs and global arc inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph with \(\ell:A\to\mathbb R\), fix \(s\in V\), and assume every vertex is reachable from \(s\). Let \(T\subseteq A\) be a spanning arborescence rooted at \(s\), with parent \(p(v)\) for each \(v\in V\setminus\{s\}\), and let \(d:V\to\mathbb R\). The pair \((T,d)\) is a shortest-path-tree certificate if \(d(s)=0\),
\[d(v)=d(p(v))+\ell(p(v),v)\qquad(v\in V\setminus\{s\}),\]
and
\[d(v)\le d(u)+\ell(u,v)\qquad((u,v)\in A).\]
Under these conditions, \(d(v)=d_s(v)\) for every \(v\in V\), and the unique \(s\)-to-\(v\) path in \(T\) is shortest for every \(v\in V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tight parent arcs together with valid inequalities on every graph arc certify all source distances and all paths in the rooted shortest-path tree.
assumptions_latex: \(s\in V\), and every vertex is reachable from \(s\).
\(T\subseteq A\) is a spanning arborescence rooted at \(s\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d(v)=d_s(v)\) for every \(v\in V\), and every rooted tree path in \(T\) is shortest.

notation.meaning: candidate spanning arborescence rooted at s

knowledge_statements.title: Negative-Cycle Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certifies that shortest-walk values are unbounded below through an explicit reachable negative cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph with \(\ell:A\to\mathbb R\), and fix \(s\in V\). A negative-cycle certificate consists of a directed path from \(s\) to a vertex \(v_0\) and a directed cycle \(C=(v_0,v_1,\ldots,v_k=v_0)\) satisfying
\[\ell(C)=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\ell(v_{i-1},v_i)<0.\]
For \(t\in V\), define the shortest-walk value
\[d_s^{\mathrm{walk}}(t)=\inf\{\ell(W):W\text{ is a directed walk from }s\text{ to }t\}.\]
For every vertex \(t\) reachable from \(C\), the certificate establishes \(d_s^{\mathrm{walk}}(t)=-\infty\), so no minimum-length directed \(s\)-to-\(t\) walk exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A source-reachable directed cycle of negative total length certifies that every downstream shortest-walk value is unbounded below.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a directed cycle reachable from \(s\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every vertex \(t\) reachable from \(C\), \(d_s^{\mathrm{walk}}(t)=-\infty\).

notation.meaning: infimum of lengths of directed s-to-t walks

knowledge_statements.title: Shortest-Path Linear-Programming Duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives the single-pair path-flow primal and vertex-potential dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph with \(\ell:A\to\mathbb R\), and let distinct vertices \(s,t\in V\) satisfy that a directed \(s\)-to-\(t\) path exists. Assume that \(G\) has no negative directed cycle. Define \(b_s=1\), \(b_t=-1\), and \(b_v=0\) for \(v\in V\setminus\{s,t\}\). The shortest \(s\)-to-\(t\) path length equals
\[\min\left\{\sum_{a\in A}\ell(a)x_a:\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}x_a-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}x_a=b_v\ \text{for every }v\in V,\ x_a\ge0\ \text{for every }a\in A\right\}.\]
Its linear-programming dual is
\[\max\left\{\pi(t)-\pi(s):\pi:V\to\mathbb R,\ \pi(v)-\pi(u)\le\ell(u,v)\ \text{for every }(u,v)\in A\right\}.\]
Both optima are attained and equal, and an optimal primal solution can be chosen as the incidence vector of a shortest directed \(s\)-to-\(t\) path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimum-cost nonnegative unit-flow formulation and the maximum feasible potential-difference formulation have equal optima, equal to the shortest source-target path length.
assumptions_latex: \(s,t\in V\), \(s\ne t\), and a directed \(s\)-to-\(t\) path exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed unit-flow minimum and feasible-potential maximum are attained and equal to \(d_s(t)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Breadth-First Search for Unit Lengths
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies single-source BFS for directed or undirected unit-length graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite graph \(G=(V,A)\) with \(\ell(a)=1\) for every arc and source \(s\), initialize \(d(s)=0\), \(d(v)=+\infty\) for \(v\ne s\), and a FIFO queue containing \(s\). Repeatedly remove the queue front \(u\). For each outgoing arc \((u,v)\), if \(d(v)=+\infty\), set \(d(v)=d(u)+1\), set \(p(v)=u\), and append \(v\). Stop when the queue is empty. The labels are shortest-path lengths, and the parent arcs form a shortest-path tree on the reachable vertices. With adjacency lists, the running time is \(O(|V|+|A|)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: BFS discovers vertices by increasing numbers of arcs, producing unit-length distances and a shortest-path tree in linear time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d(v)=d_s(v)\) for every \(v\in V\), in \(O(|V|+|A|)\) time with adjacency lists.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A rooted tree that simultaneously represents shortest paths from one source to every reachable vertex.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Breadth-First Distance-Layer Construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Successive distance layers for directed shortest paths whose length is the number of arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a digraph \(D=(V,A)\) and source \(s\), set \(V_0=\{s\}\). For \(i\ge 0\), set \[V_{i+1}=\left\{v\in V\setminus\bigcup_{j=0}^{i}V_j:\exists u\in V_i\text{ with }(u,v)\in A\right\}.\] Continue until \(V_{i+1}=\varnothing\). Then \(V_i\) is the set of vertices at distance \(i\) from \(s\), and the layers can be determined in linear time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start with the source and repeatedly collect the previously undiscovered out-neighbors of the current layer. Layer i is exactly the set of vertices at distance i from the source, and all layers can be computed in linear time.
assumptions_latex: \text{path length is measured by the number of arcs}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: V_i=\{v\in V:\operatorname{dist}_D(s,v)=i\}\text{ for every generated layer, and the layers are computable in }O(|V|+|A|)\text{ time}.

knowledge_statements.title: Topological Shortest Paths in Acyclic Networks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies one-pass relaxation in topological order for weighted directed acyclic graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite directed acyclic graph \(G=(V,A)\), arbitrary real arc lengths, and source \(s\), compute a topological ordering \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\). Initialize \(d(s)=0\) and \(d(v)=+\infty\) for \(v\ne s\). Process vertices in topological order; when processing \(u\), relax every outgoing arc \((u,v)\) by replacing \(d(v)\) with \(\min\{d(v),d(u)+\ell(u,v)\}\), recording \(u\) as parent after a strict improvement. After the single pass, \(d(v)\) is the shortest distance from \(s\) to \(v\). The running time is \(O(|V|+|A|)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a DAG, relaxing outgoing arcs once in topological order computes shortest distances even when arc lengths are negative.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is a finite directed acyclic graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d(v)=d_s(v)\) for all \(v\in V\), with running time \(O(|V|+|A|)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-source shortest paths in a directed acyclic network; arc costs need not be nonnegative.

knowledge_statements.title: Generic Relaxation Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States an edge-relaxation scheme with Bellman–Ford passes and cycle detection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(G=(V,A)\), lengths \(\ell\), and source \(s\), initialize \(d(s)=0\) and \(d(v)=+\infty\) for \(v\ne s\). A relaxation of \((u,v)\) replaces \(d(v)\) by \(d(u)+\ell(u,v)\) whenever this value is smaller, and records predecessor \(u\). Perform \(|V|-1\) complete passes through \(A\), permitting any fixed arc order, and stop early if a pass changes no label. If no reachable negative cycle exists, the final labels are exact shortest distances. A further successful relaxation certifies the existence of a negative directed cycle reachable from \(s\). The running time is \(O(|V||A|)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeated arc relaxation computes single-source distances and detects source-reachable negative cycles through an additional successful pass.

knowledge_statements.title: Dense-Graph Dijkstra Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case array-and-matrix implementation of single-source Dijkstra on nonnegative lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(d(s)=0\) and \(d(v)=+\infty\) for every \(v\in V\setminus\{s\}\). In each of at most \(n\) iterations, scan the unsettled vertices to select one with minimum tentative label, settle it, and scan its entire adjacency-matrix row to perform relaxations. The selections and row scans each take \(\Theta(n^2)\) time over the execution. Thus this dense-graph implementation runs in \(\Theta(n^2)\) time, uses \(\Theta(n^2)\) space for the matrix, and uses \(O(n)\) additional space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With unsorted-array selection and complete adjacency-matrix row scans, Dijkstra runs in quadratic time, uses quadratic graph-storage space, and uses linear additional space.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite directed graph with \(n=|V|\), nonnegative arc lengths \(w:E\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\), and source \(s\in V\).
The graph is stored as an \(n\)-by-\(n\) adjacency matrix, and tentative labels are stored in an unsorted vertex array.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The implementation runs in \(\Theta(n^2)\) time, uses \(\Theta(n^2)\) graph-representation space, and uses \(O(n)\) auxiliary space.

knowledge_statements.title: Array-Based Priority Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unsorted-array realization of Dijkstra's minimum-label selection operation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(d(s)=0\), set \(d(v)=+\infty\) for every \(v\in V\setminus\{s\}\), and set \(S=\varnothing\). While an unsettled vertex has a finite label, scan the vertex array to choose \(u\in V\setminus S\) minimizing \(d(u)\), add \(u\) to \(S\), and, for every outgoing arc \((u,v)\in E\), replace \(d(v)\) by \(\min\{d(v),d(u)+w(u,v)\}\), recording a predecessor when the label decreases. Stop when no unsettled vertex has a finite label. The final labels are the shortest-path distances from \(s\), and the recorded predecessors recover shortest paths to reachable vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dijkstra may select each next vertex by scanning an unsorted label array. It returns shortest-path distances and predecessor paths in O(n squared plus m) time while using O(n) auxiliary space beyond the graph.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite directed graph with \(n=|V|\), \(m=|E|\), source \(s\in V\), and nonnegative arc lengths \(w:E\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\).
Outgoing arcs are enumerable in total \(O(m)\) time, and tentative labels and settled indicators are stored in arrays indexed by vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The implementation returns shortest-path distances from \(s\) in \(O(n^2+m)\) time and uses \(O(n)\) auxiliary space beyond the graph representation.

children.top_down_role: Performance boundaries relating graph density to storage and priority representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Density–Representation Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic comparison including the graph representation used by each priority-selection strategy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With an adjacency matrix and unsorted-array priority selection, Dijkstra runs in \(\Theta(n^2)\) time and uses \(\Theta(n^2)\) graph-representation space. With adjacency lists and a binary heap supporting decrease-key, it runs in \(O((m+n)\log n)\) time and uses \(O(m+n)\) graph-plus-queue space. The displayed heap bound is \(o(n^2)\) when \((m+n)\log n=o(n^2)\), as in sufficiently sparse regimes. When \(m=\Theta(n^2)\), the displayed bounds are \(\Theta(n^2)\) for the array-and-matrix implementation and \(O(n^2\log n)\) for the binary-heap implementation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adjacency lists with a binary heap have the better displayed asymptotic bound in sufficiently sparse graphs, while an adjacency matrix with array selection gives quadratic time and avoids the heap's logarithmic factor in the usual dense regime.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite directed graph with \(n=|V|\), \(m=|E|\), and nonnegative arc lengths.
The compared implementations use an adjacency matrix with unsorted-array selection or adjacency lists with a binary heap supporting decrease-key.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The respective bounds are \(T_{\mathrm{arr}}=\Theta(n^2)\) and \(T_{\mathrm{heap}}=O((m+n)\log n)\), with representation spaces \(\Theta(n^2)\) and \(O(m+n)\); their comparison therefore depends on graph density and representation.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Store each unsettled vertex with finite tentative distance in a binary min-heap keyed by \(d(v)\). Dijkstra performs at most \(n\) insertions, \(n\) extract-min operations, and \(m\) successful or attempted relaxations, of which at most \(m\) invoke decrease-key. Each heap operation costs \(O(\log n)\), while adjacency-list scanning costs \(O(m)\). Therefore the total running time is \(O((m+n)\log n)\), commonly written \(O(m\log n)\) when all reachable vertices are incident to scanned arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary heap implements Dijkstra in logarithmic time per priority update or extraction, yielding near-linear-logarithmic total time on sparse graphs.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-front Dijkstra with the standard lower-bound stopping rule for one source-target query.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize forward Dijkstra at \(s\), backward Dijkstra at \(t\), and \(\mu=+\infty\). Alternate or otherwise choose valid minimum-key extractions from the two queues. Whenever scanning an arc or meeting vertex connects labels from opposite searches, update \(\mu\) with the resulting complete \(s\)-to-\(t\) walk length. Let \(k_f\) and \(k_b\) be the current minimum unsettled keys. Stop when a finite \(\mu\) satisfies \(k_f+k_b\ge\mu\), or when a queue empties. Return \(\mu\), with infinity denoting that no path exists.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bidirectional Dijkstra Search and Path Reconstruction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Point-to-point shortest paths obtained by alternating forward and reverse label-setting searches.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a directed network with nonnegative arc lengths, run forward Dijkstra from $s$ and reverse Dijkstra from $t$, alternately making one minimum temporary label permanent in each search until their permanent sets first intersect at a node $k$. Let $P(i)$ be the settled shortest path from $s$ to $i\in S$ and $P'(j)$ the settled shortest path from $j\in S'$ to $t$. Then a shortest $s$-$t$ path is either $P(k)\cup P'(k)$ or $P(i)\cup\{(i,j)\}\cup P'(j)$ for some arc $(i,j)$ with $i\in S$ and $j\in S'$. Thus its length is the minimum over these candidates. The method may settle fewer nodes in practice, but no better worst-case bound is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Alternate forward Dijkstra steps from the source with reverse Dijkstra steps from the target until their permanent sets first meet. A shortest path is obtained either by joining the searches at the common node or across an arc from the forward permanent set to the reverse permanent set. The method can reduce work in practice but has no asserted worst-case improvement.
assumptions_latex: G=(N,A)\text{ is a directed network with specified nodes }s,t.
S\cap S'=\{k\}\text{ when the permanent sets first intersect.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dist}(s,t)=\min\!\left\{\ell(P(k))+\ell(P'(k)),\ \min_{\substack{(i,j)\in A\\ i\in S,\ j\in S'}}\left(\ell(P(i))+c_{ij}+\ell(P'(j))\right)\right\}.

children.title: Dial Priority Queues

knowledge_statements.title: Dial Priority Queues
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cyclic Dial buckets for bounded nonnegative integer arc lengths with positive maximum bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize the tentative distance of \(s\) to \(0\) and all other tentative distances to \(+\infty\). Maintain \(C+1\) cyclic buckets, placing each active vertex with finite tentative distance \(x\) in \(B_{x\bmod(C+1)}\). Starting from the last extracted key \(D\), advance through integer key positions until finding a bucket containing an active entry with the current key; reject stale copies when duplicate entries are used. Extract that vertex and relax its outgoing arcs, relocating or reinserting every vertex whose integer label decreases. For an extracted key \(D\), every newly generated key lies between \(D\) and \(D+C\), so the cyclic bucket index identifies the correct pending key range.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For integer arc lengths bounded by a positive integer C, Dial's cyclic queue stores active distance labels in C plus one buckets and extracts them in nondecreasing order, giving O(m plus nC) Dijkstra time and O(n plus C) auxiliary space.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite directed graph with \(n=|V|\), \(m=|E|\), and source \(s\in V\).
The arc-length function satisfies \(w:E\to\{0,1,\ldots,C\}\) for an integer \(C\ge 1\).
Dijkstra extractions have nondecreasing finite keys.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Using Dial's cyclic priority queue, Dijkstra runs in \(O(m+nC)\) time and uses \(O(n+C)\) auxiliary space.

notation.meaning: Ordered key ranges assigned to buckets

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Invariant shared by exact-key, cyclic, duplicate-entry, and range-bucket queues.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition the admissible key domain into ordered intervals \(I_0,I_1,\ldots\), and store each active item in a bucket whose interval contains its current key. Extraction scans buckets in interval order, skipping empty or stale entries. Before returning an item, the implementation must ensure that no active item lies in an earlier interval and must select an exact minimum within the first eligible interval unless all its active keys are equal. Decrease-key either relocates the item or inserts a new copy while marking older copies stale. These invariants represent a correct monotone min-priority queue.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bucket queues may vary their ranges and update policy, but extraction must still return an exact active minimum and safely reject stale entries.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) has \(n\) vertices, \(m\) arcs, and integer lengths in \(\{0,\ldots,C\}\).
The source is fixed and only reachable vertices are processed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dial's range regime gives \(O(m+nC)\) time and \(O(n+C)\) auxiliary space; dependence on \(C\) is pseudo-polynomial.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every finite shortest-path distance is at most \(U=(n-1)C\), because a shortest path may be chosen simple. A direct array of buckets for keys \(0,\ldots,U\) uses \(O(nC)\) bucket headers, whereas cyclic Dial storage uses only \(C+1\) buckets. During monotone extraction, the scan advances over at most \(O(nC)\) integer positions, and all arc relaxations cost \(O(m)\). Thus cyclic Dial Dijkstra uses \(O(m+nC)\) time and \(O(n+C)\) auxiliary space, which is polynomial in \(C\) rather than in its bit length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dial buckets are efficient when the maximum integer edge length is small, but their linear dependence on that value is pseudo-polynomial.

assumptions_latex: Priority keys are monotone integers in \(\{0,1,\ldots,U\}\).
A radix heap groups keys by the most significant bit in which they differ from the last extracted key.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A radix heap processes \(N\) queue operations in \(O(N\log(U+1))\) amortized time using \(O(N+\log(U+1))\) space.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Amortized monotone integer-priority-queue bound used within Dijkstra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain \(O(\log(U+1))\) buckets determined by the highest differing bit between a key and the last extracted key \(D\), with a separate bucket for key \(D\). Insert or decrease-key places an item according to this index. To extract a minimum when the zero-difference bucket is empty, find the first nonempty bucket, set \(D\) to its minimum key, redistribute that bucket under the new \(D\), and then extract from the zero-difference bucket. Each item moves through only \(O(\log(U+1))\) bucket levels, yielding the amortized bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A radix heap exploits nondecreasing integer keys, redistributing items by differing bit positions to obtain logarithmic dependence on the key universe.
knowledge_statements.title: Radix-Heap Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation supports the radix-heap redistribution invariant or the stated sequence and space bounds, so the complexity claim cannot yet be admitted.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) has nonnegative arc lengths, source \(s\), and target \(t\).
The heuristic satisfies \(h(t)=0\) and \(h(u)\le w(u,v)+h(v)\) for every arc \((u,v)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: When \(t\) is extracted, \(g(t)=\operatorname{dist}_G(s,t)\), and no settled vertex requires reopening.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-search A-star with a consistent heuristic and no vertex reopening.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(g(s)=0\), set \(g(v)=+\infty\) for \(v\ne s\), and insert \(s\) with key \(f(s)=g(s)+h(s)\). Repeatedly extract an unsettled vertex \(u\) of minimum \(f(u)\), settle it, and relax every outgoing arc by replacing \(g(v)\) with \(\min\{g(v),g(u)+w(u,v)\}\), updating its predecessor and queue key when improved. Stop and return the predecessor path when \(t\) is extracted; report failure if the queue empties. Heuristic consistency makes reduced arc lengths nonnegative, so settled labels are final.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A-star orders vertices by tentative distance plus a consistent target estimate; consistency makes its label-setting extractions final and yields an optimal target path.
knowledge_statements.title: A-Star Family

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The graph-search A-star finality and no-reopening conclusions are plausible under consistency, but no authoritative locator is supplied for the exact algorithm and conclusion.

assumptions_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite directed graph with source \(s\), target \(t\), and arc lengths \(c:E\to\mathbb{R}\).
Forward and backward heuristics \(h_f,h_b\) are balanced, \(h_f(v)+h_b(v)=K\), and induce nonnegative reduced arc lengths.
Both searches use label-setting extraction, and \(\mu\) is the best complete path length found.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Run one heuristic search from \(s\) and one on the reversed graph from \(t\). Let \(F_f\) and \(F_b\) be the minimum open keys \(g_f(v)+h_f(v)\) and \(g_b(v)+h_b(v)\), respectively. Whenever the searches meet across a vertex or arc, update \(\mu\) with the corresponding complete-path length. Terminate when \[F_f+F_b\geq \mu+K.\] Then \(\mu=d(s,t)\); if no meeting produces a finite \(\mu\), no \(s\)-to-\(t\) path exists.

notation.meaning: Best path length found through a meeting of the two searches

children.title: Heuristic Accuracy Regimes
children.top_down_role: Search behavior across differing levels of heuristic informativeness.

knowledge_statements.title: Heuristic Accuracy Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise admissible, additive-error, multiplicative-error, and exact heuristic regimes on vertices with finite nonnegative target distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R=\{v\in V:d(v,t)<+\infty\}\), and suppose \(d(v,t)\geq 0\) for every \(v\in R\). The heuristic is admissible when \(h(v)\leq d(v,t)\) for every \(v\in V\); it is \(\varepsilon\)-additively accurate, for \(\varepsilon\geq0\), when \(0\leq d(v,t)-h(v)\leq\varepsilon\) for every \(v\in R\); it is \(\rho\)-multiplicatively accurate, for \(\rho\geq1\), when \(d(v,t)/\rho\leq h(v)\leq d(v,t)\) for every \(v\in R\); and it is exact on \(R\) when \(h(v)=d(v,t)\) for every \(v\in R\). Exactness implies every such additive and multiplicative bound, whereas admissibility alone supplies no uniform finite error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On vertices with finite nonnegative target distance, heuristic quality ranges from admissibility through bounded additive or multiplicative error to exact distance information.
assumptions_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite directed graph with target \(t\), and let \(d(v,t)\in\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be the shortest-path distance to \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Let \(R=\{v\in V:d(v,t)<+\infty\}\), and suppose \(d(v,t)\geq 0\) for every \(v\in R\). children.title: Heuristic Consistency Boundary
children.top_down_role: Structural boundary separating consistency-preserving search from inconsistent guidance.

assumptions_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) have arc lengths \(c(u,v)\), target \(t\), and heuristic \(h:V\to\mathbb{R}\) with \(h(t)=0\).
Shortest-path distances to \(t\) are well defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The consistency boundary is the system \[h(u)\leq c(u,v)+h(v)\qquad\text{for every }(u,v)\in E.\] Equivalently, every reduced length \(c_h(u,v)=c(u,v)+h(v)-h(u)\) is nonnegative. Consistency implies admissibility on every vertex that reaches \(t\). Consequently, A-star keys are nondecreasing along paths, and a vertex extracted with minimum key need not be reopened. If the inequality fails, admissibility alone does not ensure this label-setting property.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-search consistency characterized by nonnegative heuristic-reduced arc lengths.

children.title: Node-Reopening Regimes
children.top_down_role: Search regimes in which previously processed vertices may require renewed consideration.

knowledge_statements.title: Node-Reopening Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph A-star regimes distinguished by whether improved closed labels are reopened.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(h\) is consistent, every minimum-key extraction permanently fixes \(g(v)=d(s,v)\), so closed vertices need not be reopened. If \(h\) is admissible but inconsistent, whenever relaxation produces \(g_{\mathrm{new}}(v)<g(v)\) for a closed vertex \(v\), the general reopening regime returns \(v\) to the open set. Under this rule, extracting \(t\) with minimum key returns \(g(t)=d(s,t)\). If reopenings are suppressed for an inconsistent heuristic, the returned target cost can be suboptimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Consistent heuristics permit permanent closure, while admissible inconsistent heuristics generally require reopening a closed vertex whenever its source-cost label improves.
assumptions_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite directed graph with source \(s\), target \(t\), arc lengths \(c:E\to\mathbb{R}\), and no negative-length cycle reachable from \(s\).
Let \(h:V\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfy \(h(t)=0\) and \(h(v)\leq d(v,t)\) whenever \(t\) is reachable from \(v\).
A-star graph search maintains tentative source costs \(g(v)\), extracts a minimum key \(g(v)+h(v)\), relaxes outgoing arcs, and maintains open and closed sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(h\) is consistent, every minimum-key extraction permanently fixes \(g(v)=d(s,v)\), so closed vertices need not be reopened. If \(h\) is admissible but inconsistent, whenever relaxation produces \(g_{\mathrm{new}}(v)<g(v)\) for a closed vertex \(v\), the general reopening regime returns \(v\) to the open set. Under this rule, extracting \(t\) with minimum key returns \(g(t)=d(s,t)\). If reopenings are suppressed for an inconsistent heuristic, the returned target cost can be suboptimal.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Modified Active-List Label-Correcting Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Label-correcting implementation that processes outgoing arcs from active nodes and reactivates a node after its label improves. The removal order and any termination, correctness, or complexity guarantee are unspecified.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a directed network \(G=(N,A)\), source \(s\), arc lengths \(c_{ij}\), and outgoing-arc sets \(A(i)\), initialize \(d(s):=0\), \(\operatorname{pred}(s):=0\), \(d(j):=\infty\) for each \(j\in N\setminus\{s\}\), and \(\mathrm{LIST}:=\{s\}\). While \(\mathrm{LIST}\ne\varnothing\), remove an element \(i\) and, for every \((i,j)\in A(i)\) satisfying \(d(j)>d(i)+c_{ij}\), set \(d(j):=d(i)+c_{ij}\), set \(\operatorname{pred}(j):=i\), and add \(j\) to \(\mathrm{LIST}\) if it is not already present.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Begin with the source active. Repeatedly remove an active node, relax its outgoing arcs, and add each newly improved head node to the active list unless it is already present.
assumptions_latex: c_{ij}\text{ is specified for every }(i,j)\in A
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathrm{LIST}=\varnothing\text{ is the algorithm's stopping condition.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Synchronous Bellman label-correcting iteration for rooted shortest paths
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the synchronous length-bounded Bellman iteration, its finite-round invariant and work bound, and the tight-arc route representation. Bellman equations alone need not uniquely determine unreachable labels when zero-length cycles are present; initialization at infinity selects the shortest-path distances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(\mathcal N,\mathcal A)\) be a finite directed network with root \(r\) and nonnegative arc lengths. Set \(v_r^{(0)}=0\) and \(v_i^{(0)}=+\infty\) for \(i\ne r\), and update synchronously by \(v_r^{(k+1)}=0\) and \(v_i^{(k+1)}=\min_{(i,j)\in\mathcal A}(c_{ij}+v_j^{(k)})\). Then \(v_i^{(k)}\) is the minimum length of an \(i\)-to-\(r\) directed path using at most \(k\) arcs. Hence the correct distances are obtained after at most \(|\mathcal N|-1\) rounds and stabilization is detected within at most \(|\mathcal N|\) updates, using \(O(|\mathcal N||\mathcal A|)\) additions and comparisons. For finite distances, the tight arcs \(\mathcal T=\{(i,j):d(i,r)=c_{ij}+d(j,r)\}\) can contain alternatives and need not form a tree; every directed path in \(\mathcal T\) that ends at \(r\) is shortest.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting with zero at the root and infinity elsewhere, synchronous Bellman updates compute the shortest route using successively larger arc limits. They obtain all shortest-path distances after at most one fewer round than the number of nodes, with node-times-arc work. Equality arcs can represent several shortest routes and need not form a tree.
assumptions_latex: G=(\mathcal N,\mathcal A)\text{ is a finite directed network}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v_i^{(k)}=\min_{P:i\leadsto r,\ |P|\le k}\sum_{a\in P}c_a,\qquad v_i^{(|\mathcal N|-1)}=d(i,r),\qquad \text{work}=O(|\mathcal N||\mathcal A|)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Moore–Bellman–Ford Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-source shortest paths with arbitrary real edge weights and detection of a reachable negative directed circuit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize $\ell(s)=0$ and $\ell(v)=\infty$ for $v\ne s$. For $n-1$ passes, relax every edge $(v,w)$ by setting $(\ell(w),p(w))=(\ell(v)+c(v,w),v)$ whenever $\ell(w)>\ell(v)+c(v,w)$. Afterward, if an edge remains relaxable, construct and output a directed circuit from the resulting predecessor walk; otherwise output the labels and predecessors as shortest-path distances and paths. Unreachable vertices retain label $\infty$ and undefined predecessors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Moore–Bellman–Ford performs n−1 complete edge-relaxation passes. A subsequent possible relaxation produces a reachable negative circuit through predecessor tracing; otherwise the labels and predecessors describe shortest paths from the source.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The algorithm outputs either a negative directed circuit reachable from }s\text{ or shortest-path labels and predecessors from }s

knowledge_statements.title: Yen Label-Correcting Modifications
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Yen's alternating forward/backward ordered relaxation modification of Bellman-Ford.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition \(E\) into \(E^+=\{(v_i,v_j)\in E:i<j\}\) and \(E^-=\{(v_i,v_j)\in E:i\geq j\}\). Initialize \(d(s)=0\) and \(d(v)=+\infty\) for \(v\ne s\). In each round, scan tails in increasing index while relaxing arcs in \(E^+\), and then scan tails in decreasing index while relaxing arcs in \(E^-\), using every updated label immediately. Stop when a complete round changes no label. The final labels equal the shortest-path distances from \(s\), and the worst-case running time is \(O(|V||E|)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Yen's modification partitions arcs by a vertex ordering and alternates forward and backward relaxation scans, using improvements immediately while retaining the Bellman–Ford worst-case bound.

children.title: Small-Label-First Ordering
children.top_down_role: Active-list ordering biased toward vertices with smaller current labels.

assumptions_latex: A label-correcting shortest-path method maintains a nonempty deque \(Q\) of active vertices with tentative labels \(d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: When an inactive vertex \(v\) becomes active, compare \(d(v)\) with the label \(d(f)\) of the current front vertex \(f\). Insert \(v\) at the front if \(d(v)<d(f)\), and at the rear otherwise; if \(Q\) was empty, insert \(v\) as its sole element. Processing and relaxation rules remain unchanged. Thus the smallest of the newly inserted label and the former front label is processed next, without maintaining a globally sorted priority queue.

children.title: Large-Label-Last Ordering
children.top_down_role: Active-list ordering that postpones vertices with comparatively large labels.

assumptions_latex: A label-correcting method maintains a deque \(Q\) of active vertices, each having finite tentative label \(d(v)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Before removing a vertex for scanning, compute the active-label mean \[\bar d_Q=\frac{1}{|Q|}\sum_{v\in Q}d(v).\] While the front vertex \(f\) satisfies \(d(f)>\bar d_Q\), move \(f\) to the rear and inspect the new front, stopping after at most one complete traversal. Remove and scan the first front vertex with \(d(f)\leq\bar d_Q\). The rule delays relatively large labels while preserving every active vertex and hence preserves correctness of the underlying terminating label-correcting method.

children.title: Combined Label-Ordering Regimes
children.top_down_role: Active-list variants combining both label-based ordering preferences.

assumptions_latex: A terminating deque-based label-correcting method maintains tentative labels \(d\) and active deque \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Apply small-label-first whenever an improved inactive vertex is inserted: prepend it exactly when its label is below the current front label. Apply large-label-last before each extraction: rotate front vertices whose labels exceed \(\bar d_Q=|Q|^{-1}\sum_{v\in Q}d(v)\). The combined regime changes only active-list order, not relaxations or membership. Therefore, when the deque becomes empty, the labels satisfy all arc optimality inequalities and equal the shortest-path distances under the usual no-reachable-negative-cycle assumption.

knowledge_statements.title: Queue Disciplines
knowledge_statements.scope_note: FIFO active-list discipline for generic label-correcting shortest-path methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(d(s)=0\), \(d(v)=+\infty\) for \(v\ne s\), and the FIFO queue \(Q\) with \(s\). Repeatedly remove the front vertex \(u\), relax every outgoing arc \((u,v)\), and append \(v\) at the rear whenever its label strictly decreases and it is not already active. When \(Q\) becomes empty, no arc is relaxable and \(d(v)=\operatorname{dist}(s,v)\) for every \(v\in V\). The FIFO discipline changes processing order but not the general worst-case guarantee of label correction.

knowledge_statements.title: Deque Disciplines
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic double-ended active-list representation for label-correcting shortest-path disciplines.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A deque discipline represents the active set by a double-ended queue \(Q\). Starting from \(d(s)=0\), \(d(v)=+\infty\) for \(v\ne s\), and \(Q=(s)\), each iteration removes a prescribed end vertex, relaxes all of its outgoing arcs, and inserts every improved inactive vertex at the front or rear according to a fixed state- or label-dependent rule. If every active vertex is eventually processed and no improved inactive vertex is omitted, termination with \(Q\) empty implies that no arc is relaxable and that \(d(v)=\operatorname{dist}(s,v)\) for every \(v\in V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deque discipline represents the active set with two-ended insertion and removal; with standard label-correcting initialization and fair processing, empty-deque termination yields shortest-path labels.
assumptions_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite directed graph with source \(s\), arc-length map \(c:E\to\mathbb{R}\), and no negative-length cycle reachable from \(s\).
At most one active occurrence of each vertex is stored, and every strict label improvement activates an inactive vertex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A deque discipline represents the active set by a double-ended queue \(Q\). Starting from \(d(s)=0\), \(d(v)=+\infty\) for \(v\ne s\), and \(Q=(s)\), each iteration removes a prescribed end vertex, relaxes all of its outgoing arcs, and inserts every improved inactive vertex at the front or rear according to a fixed state- or label-dependent rule. children.title: Stack Disciplines
children.top_down_role: Last-in-first-out active-list organization for label correction.

knowledge_statements.title: Stack Disciplines
knowledge_statements.scope_note: LIFO active-list discipline for generic label-correcting shortest paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite directed graph with source \(s\), initialize \(d(s)=0\), \(d(v)=+\infty\) for \(v\ne s\), and a stack \(S=[s]\). Pop the top vertex \(u\), and for every arc \((u,v)\) satisfying \(d(v)>d(u)+c(u,v)\), set \(d(v)\leftarrow d(u)+c(u,v)\) and record predecessor \(u\). If \(v\) is not already active, push it onto \(S\). Stop when \(S\) is empty. If no negative-cost cycle is reachable from \(s\), the final labels are shortest-path distances; a reachable negative cycle may prevent termination.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Process active vertices last-in, first-out, relaxing outgoing arcs until the stack empties; without reachable negative cycles, the final labels are shortest-path distances.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite directed graph with arc costs \(c:E\to\mathbb R\).
No negative-cost directed cycle is reachable from \(s\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d(v)=\operatorname{dist}(s,v)\) for every \(v\in V\) when the stack becomes empty.

knowledge_statements.title: Threshold Label Correcting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive-threshold active-list variant with arbitrary eligible-vertex selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\Delta>0\). Initialize shortest-path labels by \(d(s)=0\) and \(d(v)=+\infty\) for \(v\ne s\), let the active set be \(A=\{s\}\), and set \(\theta=0\). While \(A\ne\varnothing\), if no \(v\in A\) satisfies \(d(v)\le\theta\), replace \(\theta\) by \(\theta+\Delta\) until one does. Remove any eligible \(u\), relax every outgoing arc, and insert each vertex whose label strictly decreases. Stop when \(A\) is empty. In a finite graph with no reachable negative-cost cycle, the output labels equal the shortest-path distances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Process only active vertices whose labels lie below a rising threshold; relax their arcs until no active vertices remain.
assumptions_latex: \(\Delta>0\), and no negative-cost cycle is reachable from \(s\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At termination, \(d(v)=\operatorname{dist}(s,v)\) for all \(v\in V\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Threshold Label-Correcting Algorithm and Nonnegative-Length Guarantee
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-queue threshold organization, limiting cases, and guarantees that specifically require nonnegative arc lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a threshold $s$, partition the candidate list into queues $Q'$ and $Q''$, with nodes having $d_j\le s$ placed in $Q'$ and nodes having $d_j>s$ placed in $Q''$. Process nodes from $Q'$ and insert each entering node at the rear of the appropriate queue according to the same comparison. When $Q'$ is exhausted, adjust $s$ and repartition the candidate list. If every arc length is nonnegative, then upon exhaustion of $Q'$ all nodes removed since the preceding repartition are permanently labeled and cannot reenter the candidate list; under this assumption the operation count is $O(NA)$. Choosing $s$ as the current minimum label gives Dijkstra's method, while choosing $s$ larger than every current label gives the generic label-correcting method. The threshold method can operate with negative arc lengths, but the permanent-label interpretation and stated bound are not asserted in that regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The threshold method divides candidates into small-label and large-label queues, processes the small-label queue, and repartitions after it empties. With nonnegative arc lengths, nodes removed during that block then become permanent and the operation count is O(NA). A minimum-label threshold gives Dijkstra's method, while a threshold above every current label gives the generic label-correcting method. The nonnegative-length guarantees do not extend merely from the algorithm's ability to operate with negative lengths.
assumptions_latex: s\text{ is the current threshold and }d_j\text{ is the current label of node }j.
N\text{ and }A\text{ are the numbers of nodes and arcs, respectively.}
\ell_{uv}\ge 0\quad\text{for every arc }(u,v)\text{ when asserting permanent labeling and the }O(NA)\text{ bound.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d_j\le s\Rightarrow j\in Q',\qquad d_j>s\Rightarrow j\in Q'';\qquad \ell\ge0\Rightarrow\bigl(\text{block removals become permanent and the operation count is }O(NA)\bigr).

knowledge_statements.title: Label-Correcting Performance Pathologies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure caused by a reachable negative-cost cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the source be \(s\), with arcs \((s,u)\), \((u,v)\), and \((v,u)\) having respective costs \(0\), \(0\), and \(-1\). The cycle \(u,v,u\) is reachable and has cost \(-1\). Each traversal yields a strictly smaller valid walk label for \(u\), so a label-correcting method that reactivates vertices after strict decreases can perform infinitely many relaxations. Thus finiteness of the graph alone does not ensure termination; excluding reachable negative-cost cycles, or explicitly detecting them, is essential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reachable negative cycle causes endlessly decreasing labels, so ordinary reactivation-based label correction need not terminate.
assumptions_latex: Relaxation reactivates a vertex whenever its label strictly decreases.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The labels of \(u\) and \(v\) are unbounded below, and the relaxation process need not terminate.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: All-Pairs Shortest-Path Optimality Conditions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient triangle inequalities for realizable path-length labels to be all-pairs shortest-path distances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose that, for every ordered pair \((i,j)\in N\times N\), \(d[i,j]\) is the length of some directed path from \(i\) to \(j\). Then the labels are all-pairs shortest-path distances if and only if
\[
d[i,j]\le d[i,k]+d[k,j]\qquad\text{for all }i,j,k\in N.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If each label d[i,j] is the length of an actual directed path from i to j, then all labels are shortest-path distances exactly when every triangle inequality d[i,j] ≤ d[i,k] + d[k,j] holds.
assumptions_latex: \forall(i,j)\in N\times N,\quad d[i,j]\text{ is the length of a directed path from }i\text{ to }j.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left(\forall i,j,\ d[i,j]=\operatorname{dist}(i,j)\right)\iff\left(\forall i,j,k,\ d[i,j]\le d[i,k]+d[k,j]\right).

knowledge_statements.title: Floyd–Warshall Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dynamic programming for all-pairs distances with possible negative arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Number the vertices \(1,\ldots,n\). Set \(D^{(0)}_{ii}=0\), set \(D^{(0)}_{ij}\) to the minimum cost of an arc from \(i\) to \(j\), and use \(+\infty\) when none exists. For \(k=1,\ldots,n\), compute \[D^{(k)}_{ij}=\min\bigl\{D^{(k-1)}_{ij},D^{(k-1)}_{ik}+D^{(k-1)}_{kj}\bigr\}.\] After phase \(k\), the entry is the minimum cost of an \(i\)-to-\(j\) walk whose internal vertices lie in \(\{1,\ldots,k\}\). If no negative cycle exists, output \(D^{(n)}\); a negative diagonal entry detects a negative cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Floyd–Warshall successively permits each vertex as an intermediate vertex, producing every pairwise distance and detecting negative cycles.
assumptions_latex: Arc costs are real, and absent arcs have value \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If no negative cycle exists, \(D^{(n)}_{ij}=\operatorname{dist}(i,j)\) for all \(i,j\in V\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Floyd–Warshall algorithm with final-edge reconstruction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The algorithm processes vertices 1 through n as permitted intermediate vertices and records final-edge predecessor information only when a shortest path exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a digraph G with V(G)=\{1,\ldots,n\} and conservative weights c:E(G)\to\mathbb{R}, initialize l_{ij}=c(i,j) for (i,j)\in E(G), l_{ij}=\infty for distinct nonarcs, l_{ii}=0, and p_{ij}=i. For j=1,\ldots,n, for every i\ne j and k\ne j, if l_{ik}>l_{ij}+l_{jk}, set l_{ik}:=l_{ij}+l_{jk} and p_{ik}:=p_{jk}. On termination, l_{ij}=\operatorname{dist}_{(G,c)}(i,j), and whenever an i-to-j shortest path exists, (p_{ij},j) is its final edge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initialize distances using arc weights, infinity for distinct nonarcs, and zero on the diagonal. Successively relax every i-to-k distance through each vertex j, copying the final-edge predecessor. The output gives all-pairs distances and final edges for existing shortest paths.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: l_{ij}=\operatorname{dist}_{(G,c)}(i,j),\qquad (p_{ij},j)\text{ is the final edge of a shortest }i\text{-to-}j\text{ path whenever one exists.}

knowledge_statements.title: Johnson Reweighting Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sparse all-pairs shortest paths using potentials and repeated Dijkstra runs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Add a new source \(q\) with zero-cost arcs to every vertex, and compute \(h(v)=\operatorname{dist}(q,v)\) by Bellman–Ford. If a negative cycle is detected, stop. Otherwise define \(c_h(u,v)=c(u,v)+h(u)-h(v)\), which is nonnegative. Run Dijkstra's algorithm from each \(s\in V\) using \(c_h\), obtaining \(d_h(s,v)\). Return \[d(s,v)=d_h(s,v)-h(s)+h(v).\] The reweighting preserves the relative costs of all walks having the same endpoints, so these recovered values are the original all-pairs shortest-path distances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Johnson computes a feasible potential, makes all arc costs nonnegative, runs Dijkstra from every source, and converts the distances back.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite directed graph with real arc costs.
The graph contains no negative-cost directed cycle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned value satisfies \(d(s,v)=\operatorname{dist}_c(s,v)\) for every ordered pair \((s,v)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Min-Plus Matrix Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: All-pairs distances as powers over the min-plus semiring.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(W\in(\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\})^{n\times n}\) have \(W_{ii}=0\) and \(W_{ij}\) equal the minimum cost of an arc from \(i\) to \(j\). Define min-plus multiplication by \[(A\otimes B)_{ij}=\min_k\{A_{ik}+B_{kj}\}.\] Then \((W^{\otimes r})_{ij}\) is the minimum cost of an \(i\)-to-\(j\) walk using at most \(r\) arcs. If the graph has no negative cycle, every finite shortest walk has a simple representative, and therefore \(W^{\otimes(n-1)}\) is the all-pairs distance matrix. Repeated squaring computes a sufficiently large power.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Min-plus matrix powers encode bounded-edge walk costs; the power with at least n−1 permitted edges gives all-pairs distances when no negative cycle exists.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) has \(n\) vertices and real arc costs.
The graph has no negative-cost directed cycle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((W^{\otimes(n-1)})_{ij}=\operatorname{dist}(i,j)\) for every \(i,j\).

notation.meaning: weighted adjacency matrix with zero diagonal

knowledge_statements.title: Repeated Single-Source Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: All-pairs distances obtained by independent single-source computations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each source \(s\in V\), run a correct single-source shortest-path algorithm under its required cost assumptions and store its output as row \(s\) of a matrix \(D\). Use Dijkstra when all arc costs are nonnegative, or a label-correcting algorithm when negative arcs are allowed but no negative cycle is reachable. After all sources have been processed, output \(D\). If one single-source run takes time \(T(n,m)\) and workspace \(S(n,m)\), the repeated method takes \(O(nT(n,m))\) time and \(O(n^2+S(n,m))\) space when the full matrix is retained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Run an appropriate single-source shortest-path algorithm from every vertex and collect the resulting distance vectors as an all-pairs matrix.

children.title: K-Shortest Walk Enumeration
children.top_down_role: Ranked shortest-walk problems permitting repeated vertices or arcs.

knowledge_statements.title: K-Shortest Walk Enumeration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Best-first enumeration of endpoint-preserving walks with strictly positive arc costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given vertices \(s,t\) and integer \(K\ge1\), initialize a min-priority queue with the zero-edge walk at \(s\), keyed by total cost. Repeatedly extract a minimum-key walk \(P\). If its last vertex is \(t\), output \(P\); otherwise append each outgoing arc of its last vertex and insert every resulting walk. Stop after \(K\) outputs or when the queue is empty. With strictly positive arc costs, only finitely many walk prefixes have cost below any fixed bound, so extraction enumerates the \(s\)-to-\(t\) walks in nondecreasing cost, counting distinct arc sequences separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform-cost search over walk prefixes outputs the K cheapest source-to-target walks, allowing repeated vertices and counting distinct arc sequences.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and \(c(e)>0\) for every \(e\in E\).
\(s,t\in V\) and \(K\) is a positive integer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The outputs \(P_1,\ldots,P_K\), when they exist, satisfy \(c(P_1)\le\cdots\le c(P_K)\) and are the first \(K\) walks in cost order.

notation.meaning: sum of arc costs along P

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Under strictly positive arc costs, the best-first walk-prefix enumeration is plausible and fits the walk-enumeration leaf, but no source or exact algorithm locator is supplied.

children.title: K-Shortest Simple-Path Enumeration
children.top_down_role: Ranked shortest-path problems restricted to simple paths.

knowledge_statements.title: K-Shortest Simple-Path Enumeration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Best-first enumeration restricted to vertex-simple path prefixes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(s,t\in V\) and \(K\ge1\), place the zero-edge path at \(s\) in a min-priority queue keyed by its cost. Repeatedly extract a minimum-key simple path \(P\). If its last vertex is \(t\), output it and do not extend it. Otherwise, for every outgoing arc to a vertex not already in \(P\), insert the extended path. Stop after \(K\) outputs or when the queue is empty. For nonnegative arc costs, every extension has cost at least its prefix, so the outputs are precisely the distinct simple \(s\)-to-\(t\) paths in nondecreasing cost order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Best-first search over vertex-simple prefixes outputs the K cheapest simple source-to-target paths, though the search space can be exponential.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and \(c(e)\ge0\) for every \(e\in E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm outputs up to \(K\) distinct simple \(s\)-to-\(t\) paths in nondecreasing cost order.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite best-first search over vertex-simple prefixes is mathematically consistent under nonnegative costs and fits the leaf, but it lacks a supporting source and exact locator.

children.title: Walk–Simplicity Boundary
children.top_down_role: Structural and computational consequences of excluding repetition.

knowledge_statements.title: Walk–Simplicity Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinction between single optimum equivalence and ranked enumeration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If every directed cycle has nonnegative cost, deleting cycles from any \(s\)-to-\(t\) walk produces a simple \(s\)-to-\(t\) path of no greater cost; hence the minimum walk cost equals the minimum simple-path cost whenever either is finite. This equivalence fails for ranked objects: adding a positive-cost self-loop at a vertex of a shortest path creates infinitely many distinct walks but no additional simple paths. If a negative-cost cycle is reachable from \(s\) and can reach \(t\), walk costs are unbounded below, whereas the finite collection of simple paths still has a minimum when nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cycle deletion equates the cheapest walk and simple path under nonnegative cycles, but ranked enumeration differs; an applicable negative cycle destroys the minimum-walk problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Walk and simple-path optimization agree at rank one under nonnegative cycles but need not agree for \(K>1\), and reachable applicable negative cycles make the walk infimum \(-\infty\).

notation.meaning: rank or requested number of objects

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cycle-deletion boundary, ranked walk/simple-path distinction, and applicable-negative-cycle conclusion are precise and fit a failure boundary, but no supporting citation is provided.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Mean Cycle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directed-cycle objective using average cost per arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite directed graph \(G=(V,E)\) with arc costs \(c:E\to\mathbb R\), the mean cost of a nonempty directed cycle \(C\) is \[\mu(C)=\frac{\sum_{e\in C}c(e)}{|C|}.\] The minimum-mean-cycle value is \[\mu^*=\min\{\mu(C):C\text{ is a directed cycle of }G\}.\] Any directed cycle attaining \(\mu^*\) is a minimum-mean cycle. If \(G\) contains no directed cycle, the optimization problem is infeasible; equivalently, its value may be assigned \(+\infty\) by convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimum-mean cycle minimizes total arc cost divided by the number of arcs among all nonempty directed cycles.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A cycle \(C^*\) is minimum-mean exactly when \(\mu(C^*)=\mu^*\).

notation.meaning: mean arc cost of cycle C
number of arcs in C, counted with multiplicity

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Ratio Cycle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directed-cycle objective with a strictly positive denominator weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a finite directed graph \(G=(V,E)\) carry numerator weights \(a:E\to\mathbb R\) and denominator weights \(b:E\to\mathbb R_{>0}\). For every nonempty directed cycle \(C\), define \[\rho(C)=\frac{\sum_{e\in C}a(e)}{\sum_{e\in C}b(e)}.\] The minimum-ratio-cycle value is \[\rho^*=\min\{\rho(C):C\text{ is a directed cycle of }G\}.\] A cycle attaining \(\rho^*\) is a minimum-ratio cycle. Strict positivity of \(b(e)\) makes every cycle denominator positive and the ratio well-defined. If no directed cycle exists, the problem is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimum-ratio cycle minimizes the sum of numerator weights divided by the positive sum of denominator weights over directed cycles.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A cycle \(C^*\) is minimum-ratio exactly when \(\rho(C^*)=\rho^*\).

notation.meaning: positive denominator weight of arc e

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The positive-denominator minimum-ratio-cycle definition is mathematically precise and fits the container, but no authoritative source or inspectable locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimum cost-to-time ratio cycle and parametric test
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the cycle-ratio objective and the transformed-length tests for a trial ratio.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(N,A)\) be a directed graph with integral arc costs \(c_{ij}\) and travel times \(\tau_{ij}\ge 0\), and suppose \(\tau(W)=\sum_{(i,j)\in W}\tau_{ij}>0\) for every directed cycle \(W\). Then
\[\mu^*=\min_{W}\frac{c(W)}{\tau(W)},\qquad c(W)=\sum_{(i,j)\in W}c_{ij}.\]
For a trial value \(\mu\), set \(l_{ij}=c_{ij}-\mu\tau_{ij}\). If some directed cycle has negative length, then \(\mu>\mu^*\). If no directed cycle has negative length and some cycle \(W^*\) has zero length, then \(\mu=\mu^*\) and \(W^*\) is optimal. If every directed cycle has positive length, then \(\mu<\mu^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimum cost-to-time ratio cycle minimizes total cost divided by positive total travel time. Under lengths equal to cost minus a trial ratio times travel time, a negative cycle shows that the trial ratio is too high; a zero cycle in the absence of negative cycles certifies optimality; and strictly positive lengths for every cycle show that the trial ratio is too low.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mu^*=\min_W\frac{c(W)}{\tau(W)},\quad l(W)<0\Rightarrow\mu>\mu^*,\quad \bigl(l(W)\ge0\ \forall W\text{ and }l(W^*)=0\bigr)\Rightarrow\mu=\mu^*,\quad l(W)>0\ \forall W\Rightarrow\mu<\mu^*.

knowledge_statements.title: Bottleneck Shortest Paths
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimax path objective on a finite directed graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite directed graph with edge weights \(w:E\to\mathbb{R}\), and let \(s,t\in V\). The bottleneck value of an \(s\)-\(t\) path \(P\) is \(b(P)=\max_{e\in P}w(e)\). A bottleneck shortest path is any path \(P^*\) satisfying \[b(P^*)=\min\{b(P):P\text{ is an }s\text{-}t\text{ path}\}.\] Equivalently, its value is the least threshold \(\lambda\) for which \(t\) is reachable from \(s\) in the subgraph \((V,\{e\in E:w(e)\leq\lambda\})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bottleneck shortest path minimizes its largest edge weight; its value is the smallest edge threshold making the target reachable.
assumptions_latex: At least one directed \(s\)-\(t\) path exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b(P^*)=\min_{P:s\leadsto t}\max_{e\in P}w(e)\).

notation.meaning: maximum edge weight on path P

children.title: Dense-Graph Complexity
children.top_down_role: Shortest-path performance in high-density graph representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Dense-Graph Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-source Dijkstra complexity with an array-based minimum selection rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) have \(n=|V|\), \(m=|E|\), and nonnegative edge lengths. Dijkstra's algorithm implemented with an unsorted array performs at most \(n\) minimum-label scans costing \(O(n)\) each and \(O(m)\) total relaxations. Its running time is therefore \(O(n^2+m)\), which is \(O(n^2)\) when \(m=\Theta(n^2)\); its storage requirement is \(O(n+m)\) under adjacency-list storage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Array-based Dijkstra runs in quadratic time on dense nonnegatively weighted graphs, with linear storage in the graph representation.
assumptions_latex: Arithmetic, comparison, and adjacency-list access take unit time.

children.title: Sparse-Graph Complexity

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse-Graph Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Heap-based single-source Dijkstra bounds for sparse graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) have \(n=|V|\), \(m=|E|\), and nonnegative edge lengths. With adjacency lists and a binary heap, Dijkstra's algorithm runs in \(O((n+m)\log n)\) time. With a Fibonacci heap, its amortized running time is \(O(m+n\log n)\). Thus, when \(m=O(n)\), these bounds become respectively \(O(n\log n)\) and \(O(n\log n)\), using \(O(n+m)\) storage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Heap implementations make Dijkstra near-linear, up to logarithmic factors, on sparse nonnegatively weighted graphs.
assumptions_latex: The graph is stored by adjacency lists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\mathrm{binary}}=O((n+m)\log n)\) and \(T_{\mathrm{Fibonacci}}=O(m+n\log n)\).

children.title: Data-Structure Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Complexity variation induced by priority, adjacency, and label-storage structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Data-Structure Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Priority-queue choice controls Dijkstra's asymptotic running time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For Dijkstra's algorithm on a graph with \(n\) vertices and \(m\) edges of nonnegative length, the priority-queue implementation changes the bound: an unsorted array gives \(O(n^2+m)\), a binary heap gives \(O((n+m)\log n)\), and a Fibonacci heap gives amortized \(O(m+n\log n)\). Consequently, arrays are asymptotically competitive on dense graphs, whereas heaps expose the advantage of sparsity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dijkstra's complexity changes from quadratic array scans to heap-sensitive bounds, so graph density determines the preferable priority queue.
assumptions_latex: The same adjacency-list relaxation scheme is used in all implementations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\mathrm{array}}=O(n^2+m)\), \(T_{\mathrm{binary}}=O((n+m)\log n)\), and \(T_{\mathrm{Fibonacci}}=O(m+n\log n)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Numeric-Magnitude Dependence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pseudo-polynomial dependence in bounded-integer shortest-path implementations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose all edge lengths are integers in \(\{0,1,\ldots,C\}\). A bucket implementation of Dijkstra's algorithm may have running time \(O(m+nC)\). This is polynomial in the numeric value \(C\) but not necessarily in its binary encoding length \(\lceil\log_2(C+1)\rceil\). Thus the bound is pseudo-polynomial: replacing \(C\) by \(2^kC\) can increase the running-time bound exponentially in the additional \(k\) input bits, although \(n\) and \(m\) are unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bound polynomial in the largest integer weight can be exponential in that weight's bit length and is therefore only pseudo-polynomial.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(O(m+nC)\) is not generally polynomial in \(n+m+\log(C+1)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Weakly Polynomial Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bit-model definition of weak polynomiality for numeric optimization problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For instances with combinatorial dimensions \(n,m\) and binary-encoded numerical data of total bit length \(L\), an algorithm is weakly polynomial when its running time is bounded by a polynomial in \(n,m,L\), but no bound polynomial solely in \(n,m\) is asserted for its arithmetic-operation count. Hence dependence polynomial in \(\log(C+1)\), where \(C\) bounds the data magnitudes, is compatible with weak polynomiality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weakly polynomial algorithm is polynomial in total input length but may depend on the bit lengths of numerical data.
assumptions_latex: Numerical input is encoded in binary.
Elementary bit operations are charged in the computation model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\leq\operatorname{poly}(n,m,L)\), possibly with essential dependence on \(L\).

children.title: Strongly Polynomial Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Polynomial Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arithmetic-model definition of strong polynomiality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An algorithm for a numerically specified combinatorial problem is strongly polynomial if the number of arithmetic and comparison operations is bounded by a polynomial in the combinatorial dimensions \(n,m\), independently of the numerical values and their encoding lengths, and every intermediate number has encoding length bounded polynomially in the input length. Under these conditions, the algorithm also has polynomial bit complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strongly polynomial algorithm uses polynomially many arithmetic operations independent of numeric magnitudes and keeps all intermediate numbers polynomially encoded.
assumptions_latex: Input numbers are rational or integral and finitely encoded.
Arithmetic and comparisons are the primitive operations counted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{ops}}\leq\operatorname{poly}(n,m)\), independently of numerical magnitudes.

notation.meaning: number of arithmetic and comparison operations

children.title: Numeric-Dependence Boundary
children.top_down_role: Boundary separating combinatorial input dependence from magnitude-sensitive performance.

knowledge_statements.title: Numeric-Dependence Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary separating pseudo-polynomial, weakly polynomial, and strongly polynomial running-time guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\geq 1\) bound the absolute values of binary-encoded numerical data. A running-time bound polynomial in \(C\) but not polynomial in the input encoding length is pseudo-polynomial. A bound polynomial in the full input encoding length may depend polynomially on \(\log(C+1)\) and is compatible with weak polynomiality. Strong polynomiality additionally requires the number of arithmetic and comparison operations to be bounded by a polynomial in the combinatorial dimensions alone, independently of \(C\) and its encoding length, with polynomially bounded intermediate encodings.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial dependence on numeric magnitudes may be only pseudo-polynomial; polynomial dependence on encoding length is compatible with weak polynomiality; strong polynomiality requires a magnitude-independent operation bound and controlled intermediate encodings.
assumptions_latex: Numerical values are encoded in binary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The forms \(\operatorname{poly}(C)\), \(\operatorname{poly}(\log(C+1))\), and magnitude-independent arithmetic-operation bounds distinguish pseudo-polynomial, weakly polynomial, and strongly polynomial guarantees subject to their respective definitions.

children.title: Negative-Cycle Obstructions

knowledge_statements.title: Negative-Cycle Obstructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finiteness criterion for minimum-weight walks between two vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite directed graph with real edge weights and vertices \(s,t\). The infimum of the weights of directed \(s\)-\(t\) walks equals \(-\infty\) if and only if some negative-weight directed cycle is reachable from \(s\) and can itself reach \(t\). If no such cycle lies on the \(s\)-\(t\) corridor and an \(s\)-\(t\) walk exists, a minimum-weight walk exists and contains no repeated cycle of negative weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shortest-walk value is unbounded below exactly when an accessible negative cycle can still reach the target.
assumptions_latex: Edge weights are real and walk weight is additive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{W:s\leadsto t}w(W)=-\infty\) exactly when a negative cycle lies on an \(s\)-\(t\) walk.

notation.meaning: sum of edge weights along walk W

knowledge_statements.title: Simple-Path Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: NP-completeness caused by imposing vertex simplicity in the presence of negative edge weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the decision problem whose input is a finite directed graph \(G=(V,E)\), vertices \(s,t\in V\), integer edge weights \(w:E\to\mathbb{Z}\), and an integer threshold \(B\): determine whether there is a simple directed \(s\)-\(t\) path \(P\) with \(w(P)\leq B\). This problem is NP-complete even when \(w(e)=-1\) for every \(e\in E\). In that case \(w(P)=-|P|\), so the threshold condition can encode the existence of a directed Hamiltonian \(s\)-\(t\) path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Requiring a shortest path to be simple makes the decision problem NP-complete with unrestricted negative weights; weights of minus one encode a longest-simple-path threshold.
assumptions_latex: The weights and \(B\) are binary-encoded integers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The decision problem \(\exists P\text{ simple directed from }s\text{ to }t:w(P)\leq B\) is NP-complete, even when \(w(e)=-1\) for every \(e\in E\).

notation.meaning: number of edges in path P

children.title: Walk–Path Complexity Boundary

knowledge_statements.title: Walk–Path Complexity Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between tractable shortest walks and hard shortest simple paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite directed graph with real edge weights, let \(s,t\in V\), and suppose an \(s\)-\(t\) walk exists. If no negative-weight directed cycle is reachable from \(s\) and able to reach \(t\), deleting repeated nonnegative-weight closed subwalks from a minimum-weight \(s\)-\(t\) walk yields a simple \(s\)-\(t\) path of no greater weight; hence the walk and simple-path optima coincide. If such a negative cycle exists, the walk infimum is \(-\infty\), whereas the simple-path optimum is finite; with unrestricted negative integer weights, computing the latter is NP-hard.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a feasible source-target pair, shortest walks and shortest simple paths coincide when no relevant negative cycle exists. With such a cycle, walks are unbounded below while the finite simple-path problem is NP-hard.
assumptions_latex: \(s,t\in V\), and at least one directed \(s\)-\(t\) walk exists.
Walk weight is the sum of real edge weights.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without a relevant negative cycle, the walk and simple-path optima are equal; with one, the walk infimum is \(-\infty\) while the simple-path optimum remains finite and is NP-hard to compute for unrestricted negative integer weights.
