knowledge_statements.statement_title: Negative-cycle walk–path complexity boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes shortest-walk behavior, flow-formulation unboundedness, and simple-path complexity when negative directed cycles occur.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a directed network contains no negative-length directed cycle, cycles can be removed from a shortest directed walk without increasing its length, so a shortest walk can be chosen to be a path. If the network contains a negative directed cycle, the referenced flow linear-programming formulation is unbounded because arbitrarily much flow can be sent around that cycle. Requiring walks not to revisit nodes produces the simple shortest-path variant, which in this regime is NP-complete.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without a negative directed cycle, some shortest walk can be made into a path by deleting cycles. A negative cycle makes the referenced flow formulation unbounded. If repeated nodes are prohibited, the resulting simple shortest-path problem in the negative-cycle regime is NP-complete.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reduction of bounded-circulation feasibility to maximum flow

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a digraph \(D=(V,A)\) and \(d,c:A\to\mathbb Q\) with \(d\le c\), set \(c'(e)=c(e)-d(e)\) for each \(e\in A\). Add vertices \(s,t\); for each \(v\) with \(\operatorname{excess}_d(v)>0\), add \((s,v)\) with capacity \(\operatorname{excess}_d(v)\), and for each \(v\) with \(\operatorname{excess}_d(v)<0\), add \((v,t)\) with capacity \(-\operatorname{excess}_d(v)\). Then \(D\) has a circulation \(f\) satisfying \(d\le f\le c\) if and only if the extended network has an \(s\)-\(t\) flow \(f'\le c'\) of value \(\sum_{v:\operatorname{excess}_d(v)>0}\operatorname{excess}_d(v)\). Recover the circulation by setting \(f(e)=f'(e)+d(e)\) for every \(e\in A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shift each original arc by its lower bound and connect a supersource and supersink to vertices with positive and negative lower-bound excess. knowledge_statements.title: Capacitated Circulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible circulation with zero lower bounds and finite arc capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite directed graph and let \(u:E\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq0}\) assign arc capacities. A capacitated circulation is a vector \(f\in\mathbb{R}^{E}\) satisfying \(0\leq f_e\leq u_e\) for every \(e\in E\) and flow conservation at every vertex: \[\sum_{e\in\delta^-(v)}f_e=\sum_{e\in\delta^+(v)}f_e\qquad(v\in V).\] The feasibility problem asks whether such an \(f\) exists; with zero lower bounds, the zero circulation is always feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A capacitated circulation respects every arc capacity and has equal total inflow and outflow at each vertex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is feasible exactly when \(0\leq f_e\leq u_e\) and flow is conserved at every vertex.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Maximum-flow circulation representation and cut capacity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents a capacitated source–sink maximum-flow problem as an augmented circulation and defines source–sink cuts and their capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $(\mathcal N,\mathcal A)$ be a directed network with source $s$, sink $t$, and finite nonnegative capacities $u_{ij}$ on its original arcs. Set the original-arc costs and all node balances to zero, and add an artificial arc $(t,s)$ with $c_{ts}=-1$ and $u_{ts}=\infty$. The resulting circulation objective is $-x_{ts}$, so minimizing it maximizes $x_{ts}$. A cut is a set $C\subseteq\mathcal N$ with $s\in C$ and $t
otin C$, and its capacity is $\kappa(C)=\sum_{i\in C,\,j
otin C}u_{ij}$, with the sum restricted to original arcs. Every feasible augmented circulation satisfies $x_{ts}=\sum_{i\in C,\,j
otin C}x_{ij}-\sum_{i
otin C,\,j\in C}x_{ij}$, again using only original arcs in the sums.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximum flow can be represented as a zero-balance circulation by adding an infinite-capacity return arc from the sink to the source with cost minus one. Minimizing circulation cost then maximizes the return-arc flow. A cut contains the source but not the sink; its capacity is the total capacity of original arcs leaving it, and flow balance makes the return-arc flow equal the net original flow crossing the cut.

C\subseteq\mathcal N,\qquad s\in C,\qquad t\notin C.
x\text{ is a feasible circulation in the augmented network.}

\min c^Tx\equiv\max x_{ts},\qquad \kappa(C)=\sum_{\substack{i\in C\j
otin C}}u_{ij},\qquad x_{ts}=\sum_{\substack{i\in C\j

knowledge_statements.title: Integral Maximum-Flow Consequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integral-capacity form of max-flow integrality and cut duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite directed graph with source \(s\), sink \(t\), and capacities \(u:E\to\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\). Then there exists a maximum \(s\)-\(t\) flow \(f\) satisfying \(f(e)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\) for every \(e\in E\). Consequently, the common max-flow/min-cut value is an integer, and an integral maximum flow decomposes into integral multiples of directed \(s\)-\(t\) path flows together with integral directed cycle flows.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite network with nonnegative integer capacities has an integral maximum flow; its value is integral and admits an integral path-and-cycle decomposition.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-pair internal-vertex connectivity in directed or undirected graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a directed or undirected graph, let \(s,t\in V(G)\) be nonadjacent, and let \(k\in\mathbb N\) with \(k\ge 1\). There exist \(k\) pairwise internally disjoint \(s\)-\(t\) paths if and only if, for every set \(X\subseteq V(G)\setminus\{s,t\}\) with \(|X|\le k-1\), \(t\) is reachable from \(s\) in \(G-X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nonadjacent vertices s and t, there are k pairwise internally disjoint s–t paths exactly when deleting any set of at most k−1 vertices other than s and t still leaves t reachable from s.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is a directed or undirected graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(\exists\ k\text{ pairwise internally disjoint }s\text{-}t\text{ paths}\bigr)\iff\bigl(\forall X\subseteq V(G)\setminus\{s,t\},\ |X|\le k-1:\ t\text{ is reachable from }s\text{ in }G-X\bigr)

knowledge_statements.title: Menger Connectivity Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite directed two-terminal edge and internally vertex-disjoint forms of Menger's theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite directed graph and let \(s,t\in V\) be distinct. The maximum number of pairwise edge-disjoint directed \(s\)-\(t\) paths equals the minimum cardinality of a set \(F\subseteq E\) such that \(G-F\) has no directed \(s\)-\(t\) path. If \(st\notin E\), the maximum number of directed \(s\)-\(t\) paths pairwise disjoint outside \(\{s,t\}\) equals the minimum cardinality of a set \(X\subseteq V\setminus\{s,t\}\) such that \(G-X\) has no directed \(s\)-\(t\) path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directed local edge connectivity equals minimum edge-separator size. If there is no arc from the source to the sink, directed local vertex connectivity equals minimum internal vertex-separator size.
assumptions_latex: \(s,t\in V\) are distinct; the vertex form additionally assumes \(st\notin E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_G(s,t)=\min\{|F|:F\subseteq E,\ G-F\text{ has no directed }s\text{-}t\text{ path}\}\), and if \(st\notin E\), then \(\kappa_G(s,t)=\min\{|X|:X\subseteq V\setminus\{s,t\},\ G-X\text{ has no directed }s\text{-}t\text{ path}\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Edge-Disjoint Path Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit-capacity flow representation of directed edge-disjoint terminal paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite directed graph \(G=(V,E)\) with terminals \(s,t\), assign capacity \(u(e)=1\) to every edge. Any family of \(k\) pairwise edge-disjoint directed \(s\)-\(t\) paths yields an integral flow of value \(k\) by summing their incidence vectors. Conversely, after deleting cycle components, every integral flow of value \(k\) decomposes into \(k\) unit path flows using no edge more than once. Hence the maximum number of edge-disjoint directed \(s\)-\(t\) paths equals the unit-capacity maximum-flow value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Edge-disjoint terminal paths are exactly the path components of integral flows in the network obtained by assigning unit capacity to every edge.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and directed, with distinct terminals \(s,t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max\{k:\text{there are }k\text{ edge-disjoint directed }s\text{-}t\text{ paths}\}=\max\{|f|:f\text{ is feasible under }u\}\).

notation.meaning: Edge-incidence vector of a directed path.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Edge-Disjoint Paths from a Packing of T-Joins
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A local edge-connectivity consequence of packing edge-disjoint parity joins.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be an undirected graph and let \(T\subseteq V(H)\) have even cardinality. If \(E(H)\) contains \(k\) pairwise edge-disjoint \(T\)-joins, then, for every \(t\in T\), there exists \(s\in V(H)\setminus\{t\}\) such that \(H\) contains \(k\) pairwise edge-disjoint \(s\)-\(t\) paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If an undirected graph contains k edge-disjoint T-joins for an even vertex set T, then every vertex t in T has some distinct vertex s joined to it by k edge-disjoint paths.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall t\in T\ \exists s\in V(H)\setminus\{t\}: H\text{ contains }k\text{ pairwise edge-disjoint }s\text{-}t\text{ paths}.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Packing–transversal equality for multiple set-pair path families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Edge-disjoint path min–max equality under pairwise disjoint complements of the terminal-set pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G=(V,E)$ and, for $i=1,\ldots,k$, let $S_i,T_i\subseteq V$ satisfy $S_i\cap T_i=\varnothing$. Define $U_i:=V\setminus(S_i\cup T_i)$. If $U_1,\ldots,U_k$ are pairwise disjoint, then the maximum number of pairwise edge-disjoint paths in $\{P:\exists i,\ P\text{ is an }S_i\text{--}T_i\text{ path}\}$ equals the minimum cardinality of an edge set intersecting every path in that family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If each source–target set pair is disjoint and the complements of their unions are pairwise disjoint, then the maximum packing of edge-disjoint admissible paths equals the minimum edge transversal of all admissible paths.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max\{|\mathcal P|:\mathcal P\text{ is a pairwise edge-disjoint subfamily of }\bigcup_{i=1}^k\mathcal P(S_i,T_i)\}=\min\{|F|:F\subseteq E,\ F\cap E(P)\ne\varnothing\ \forall P\in\bigcup_{i=1}^k\mathcal P(S_i,T_i)\}.

knowledge_statements.title: Vertex-Disjoint Path Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vertex-splitting representation of internally vertex-disjoint directed paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) have distinct terminals \(s,t\). Replace each internal vertex \(v\in V\setminus\{s,t\}\) by vertices \(v^{\mathrm{in}},v^{\mathrm{out}}\) and a capacity-one arc \(v^{\mathrm{in}}v^{\mathrm{out}}\). Replace each original arc \(vw\) by an arc from the output copy of \(v\) to the input copy of \(w\), with terminal copies interpreted naturally and capacity at least \(|V|\). Integral flows in this split network correspond, after cycle deletion, to families of directed \(s\)-\(t\) paths pairwise disjoint outside \(\{s,t\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Splitting each internal vertex through a unit-capacity arc converts internally vertex-disjoint paths into ordinary integral flows.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite directed graph with distinct terminals \(s,t\).
Only internal vertices are required to be mutually disjoint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max\{k:k\text{ internally vertex-disjoint directed }s\text{-}t\text{ paths exist}\}=\operatorname{maxflow}(G^{\mathrm{split}},s,t)\).

notation.meaning: Input and output copies of an internal vertex.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vertex-Disjoint Paths and Pairwise Vertex-Connectivity

knowledge_statements.title: Minimal Saturated Cuts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum source side determined by residual reachability from the source.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be a maximum flow and let \(G_f\) be its residual graph. Define \(S_{\min}\) as the set of vertices reachable from \(s\) in \(G_f\). Then \(t\notin S_{\min}\), every arc from \(S_{\min}\) to its complement is saturated by \(f\), and every arc entering \(S_{\min}\) carries zero flow. Thus \(\delta^+(S_{\min})\) is a minimum cut. Moreover, for every minimum-cut source side \(S\), one has \(S_{\min}\subseteq S\), so \(S_{\min}\) is the unique inclusion-minimal minimum-cut source side.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vertices residually reachable from the source form the unique smallest source side among all minimum cuts.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is a maximum flow in a finite capacitated directed network.
\(G_f\) contains exactly the residual arcs of positive residual capacity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_{\min}=\operatorname{Reach}_{G_f}(s)\) and \(S_{\min}\subseteq S\) for every minimum-cut source side \(S\).

notation.meaning: Residual graph of the maximum flow.

knowledge_statements.title: Maximal Saturated Cuts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum source side determined by reverse residual reachability to the sink.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be a maximum flow with residual graph \(G_f\). Let \(R_t\) be the set of vertices from which \(t\) is reachable in \(G_f\), and put \(S_{\max}=V\setminus R_t\). Then \(s\in S_{\max}\), \(t\notin S_{\max}\), every arc leaving \(S_{\max}\) is saturated by \(f\), and every arc entering \(S_{\max}\) carries zero flow. Hence \(\delta^+(S_{\max})\) is a minimum cut. Every minimum-cut source side \(S\) satisfies \(S\subseteq S_{\max}\), making \(S_{\max}\) uniquely inclusion-maximal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Removing vertices that can residually reach the sink gives the unique largest source side among all minimum cuts.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is a maximum flow in a finite capacitated directed network.
\(G_f\) contains exactly the residual arcs of positive residual capacity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_{\max}=V\setminus\{v:v\leadsto t\text{ in }G_f\}\) and \(S\subseteq S_{\max}\) for every minimum-cut source side \(S\).

notation.meaning: Vertices from which the sink is residually reachable.

knowledge_statements.title: Extremal-Cut Lattice Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributive lattice of minimum-cut source sides under inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite capacitated directed network, let \(\mathcal C\) be the collection of source sides of minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cuts. If \(A,B\in\mathcal C\), submodularity of directed cut capacity gives \(A\cap B\in\mathcal C\) and \(A\cup B\in\mathcal C\). Therefore \((\mathcal C,\subseteq)\) is a distributive lattice with meet \(A\wedge B=A\cap B\) and join \(A\vee B=A\cup B\). Its bottom and top elements are respectively the residual-reachability sets \(S_{\min}\) and \(S_{\max}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimum-cut source sides are closed under intersection and union, forming a distributive lattice with unique smallest and largest cuts.
assumptions_latex: The network is finite, directed, and has nonnegative capacities.
\(\mathcal C\) consists of source sides of minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cuts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\mathcal C,\cap,\cup)\) is a distributive lattice with bottom \(S_{\min}\) and top \(S_{\max}\).

notation.meaning: Extremal source sides of the minimum-cut lattice.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extremal saturated cuts under union and intersection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extremal structure of saturated source–sink cuts associated with a fixed optimal flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an optimal max-flow solution $x^*$. Let $\mathcal F$ be the family of source-side sets $\mathcal S$ for which $[\mathcal S,\mathcal N\setminus\mathcal S]$ is saturated with respect to $x^*$ and separates $s$ from $t$. Then $\bigcup_{\mathcal S\in\mathcal F}\mathcal S$ defines the maximal saturated separating cut, while $\bigcap_{\mathcal S\in\mathcal F}\mathcal S$ defines the minimal saturated separating cut. These two cuts coincide if and only if the saturated separating cut is unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed optimal flow, the union of all saturated-cut source sides gives the maximal saturated separating cut, and their intersection gives the minimal one. They coincide exactly when that cut is unique.
assumptions_latex: x^*\text{ is an optimal max-flow solution}
\mathcal F=\{\mathcal S:[\mathcal S,\mathcal N\setminus\mathcal S]\text{ is saturated with respect to }x^*\text{ and separates }s\text{ from }t\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q_{\max}=\left[\bigcup_{\mathcal S\in\mathcal F}\mathcal S,\mathcal N\setminus\bigcup_{\mathcal S\in\mathcal F}\mathcal S\right],\quad Q_{\min}=\left[\bigcap_{\mathcal S\in\mathcal F}\mathcal S,\mathcal N\setminus\bigcap_{\mathcal S\in\mathcal F}\mathcal S\right],\quad Q_{\min}=Q_{\max}\iff |\mathcal F|=1.

knowledge_statements.title: Ford–Fulkerson Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic residual augmenting-path method with arbitrary path selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a finite directed network \((G,u,s,t)\) and initialize \(f=0\). While the residual graph \(G_f\) contains a directed \(s\)-\(t\) path \(P\), set \(\Delta=\min_{e\in P}u_f(e)\) and augment \(f\) by \(\Delta\) along forward residual arcs and by \(-\Delta\) along reverse residual arcs. If no residual \(s\)-\(t\) path exists, stop and output \(f\); this output is a maximum flow. If all capacities are integral, every augmentation has \(\Delta\ge 1\), so the method terminates after at most \(|f^*|\) augmentations, where \(f^*\) is a maximum flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from zero, repeatedly augment along any residual source-to-sink path. If no such path remains, the flow is maximum; integral capacities guarantee termination after at most the maximum-flow value many augmentations.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and capacities are nonnegative.
The finite-termination bound additionally assumes \(u(e)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) for every \(e\in E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_f\text{ has no }s\text{-}t\text{ path}\Rightarrow f\text{ is maximum}\); with integral capacities and \(f=0\) initially, the number of augmentations is at most \(|f^*|\).

notation.meaning: Residual graph of the current flow.
Residual capacity of a residual arc.
Bottleneck residual capacity of the selected path.
A maximum flow, with \(|f^*|\) denoting its value.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ford–Fulkerson Labeling Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Augmenting-path maximum-flow procedure using forward and backward labeling scans.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a capacitated network \(N=(s,t,V,A,b)\), initialize \(f:=0\). Repeatedly initialize a labeling search at \(s\). When scanning a labeled vertex \(x\), label each unlabeled vertex reachable from \(x\) through an unsaturated forward arc and each unlabeled vertex whose positive-flow arc enters \(x\), recording the corresponding forward or backward predecessor. If \(t\) is labeled, augment \(f\) along the resulting augmenting path and restart; if the scan list becomes empty without labeling \(t\), terminate and output \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Begin with zero flow. Repeatedly search from the source through unsaturated arcs in their forward direction and positive-flow arcs in reverse. If the sink is reached, augment along the labeled path and restart; otherwise stop and return the current flow.
assumptions_latex: N=(s,t,V,A,b)\text{ is a capacitated flow network}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ford–Fulkerson Labeling Procedure for Finding an Augmenting Path
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual reachability search for a feasible bounded source–sink flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize $\Delta(v)=+\infty$, $L=\{v\}$, $S=\varnothing$, and $U=V(G)\setminus\{v\}$. Repeatedly remove a labeled vertex $u$ from $L$ and label each unlabeled head $h(e)$ of an outgoing edge satisfying $x_e<c(e)$ with oriented predecessor $e^+$ and value $\min\{\Delta(u),c(e)-x_e\}$, and each unlabeled tail $t(e)$ of an incoming edge satisfying $x_e>l(e)$ with oriented predecessor $e^-$ and value $\min\{\Delta(u),x_e-l(e)\}$. Return as soon as $w$ is labeled; if $L$ becomes empty, report that no augmenting path exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Ford–Fulkerson labeling search explores vertices reachable through positive forward or reverse residual slack, records oriented predecessor edges and bottleneck values, and succeeds when the sink is labeled; exhaustion certifies that no augmenting path exists.
assumptions_latex: \phi\text{ records an oriented predecessor edge for each newly labeled vertex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: w\text{ is labeled}\Rightarrow\text{an augmenting }v\text{--}w\text{ path exists};\quad L=\varnothing\Rightarrow\text{no augmenting }v\text{--}w\text{ path exists}

knowledge_statements.title: Edmonds–Karp Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shortest-residual-path specialization of Ford–Fulkerson.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a finite directed network, choose at every augmentation an \(s\)-\(t\) path having the fewest residual arcs, found by breadth-first search, and augment by its bottleneck residual capacity. Residual distances from \(s\) never decrease between augmentations. Each edge can become a critical bottleneck on at most \(O(|V|)\) distinct distance levels, so the algorithm performs \(O(|V||E|)\) augmentations. Since each breadth-first search and augmentation takes \(O(|E|)\) time, the total running time is \(O(|V||E|^2)\), independently of capacity magnitudes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choosing a shortest residual path by breadth-first search yields at most order VE augmentations and total running time order VE squared.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite directed network with nonnegative capacities.
Each augmentation uses a residual path with the minimum number of arcs.

knowledge_statements.title: Capacity-Scaling Augmentation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary residual-capacity scaling for integral maximum flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For integral capacities, initialize \(f=0\) and \(\Delta\) as the largest power of two not exceeding \(U=\max_{e\in E}u(e)\). During a \(\Delta\)-phase, retain only residual arcs with capacity at least \(\Delta\); while this subgraph contains an \(s\)-\(t\) path, augment along such a path by its full residual bottleneck. When no path remains, replace \(\Delta\) by \(\Delta/2\). Stop after completing the \(\Delta=1\) phase. The output is a maximum flow; the standard implementation uses \(O(|E|\log U)\) augmentations and \(O(|E|^2\log U)\) time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restrict augmentations to arcs above a decreasing power-of-two threshold, ending at one; this gives a maximum integral flow with logarithmically many phases.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{aug}}=O(|E|\log U)\), \(T=O(|E|^2\log U)\), and the returned flow is maximum.

knowledge_statements.title: Price-Based Augmenting Paths
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Augmenting paths constructed using feasible vertex-price labels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain a feasible flow \(f\) and vertex prices \(p:V\to\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) with \(p(t)=0\) and \(p(v)\le p(w)+1\) for every residual arc \(vw\). Initialize \(f=0\) and choose prices equal to residual distances to \(t\), using \(+\infty\) for unreachable vertices. Construct an augmenting path using admissible arcs satisfying \(p(v)=p(w)+1\). If a reached vertex has no admissible outgoing residual arc, relabel it to \(1+\min\{p(w):vw\text{ is residual}\}\). Augment on reaching \(t\); stop when \(p(s)=+\infty\), and output \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasible vertex prices identify admissible residual arcs; path construction alternates admissible advances with relabeling until augmentation or a maximum-flow certificate results.
assumptions_latex: The directed network is finite and has nonnegative capacities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p(s)=+\infty\Rightarrow G_f\text{ has no directed }s\text{-}t\text{ path}\Rightarrow f\text{ is maximum}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Irrational-Capacity Nontermination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of arbitrary-path Ford–Fulkerson termination beyond commensurable capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Ford–Fulkerson with arbitrary augmenting-path choices need not terminate when capacities are irrational. The failure mechanism is an infinite feasible augmentation sequence with bottlenecks \(\Delta_k>0\) such that \(\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\Delta_k<\infty\): every finite iterate still has a residual \(s\)-\(t\) path, while the flow values converge to a limit strictly below the maximum-flow value. Classical finite-network constructions choose capacities involving an irrational ratio and paths that implement a Euclidean-algorithm recurrence, producing infinitely many positive remainders. Thus finite termination requires a path rule or a discrete capacity unit, not merely finiteness of the network.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With irrationally related capacities, adversarial augmenting paths can generate infinitely many shrinking augmentations and converge below the maximum flow.
assumptions_latex: The network is finite but permits irrational capacities.
Augmenting paths may be selected arbitrarily.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists (G,u)\ \exists(P_k)_{k\ge1}:\ \Delta_k>0,\ \sum_k\Delta_k<\operatorname{maxflow}(G,u),\text{ and Ford--Fulkerson never terminates}\).

notation.meaning: Augmenting path selected at iteration k.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The general failure phenomenon is standard, but the stronger claim that a finite irrational-capacity example can follow an infinite augmentation sequence converging strictly below the optimum requires an authoritative locator and a concrete construction. No source is supplied.

source_refs.locator: Section 8.4. Dinic's, Karzanov's, and Fujishige's Algorithm p. 186

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite directed network with source \(s\), sink \(t\), capacities \(u:E\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\), and feasible flow \(f\), repeat: compute residual distances \(d(v)=\operatorname{dist}_{G_f}(s,v)\); if \(t\) is unreachable, output \(f\). Otherwise form the level graph \(L_f=(V,\{(v,w)\in E_f:d(w)=d(v)+1\})\), find a blocking flow \(g\) in \(L_f\), and augment \(f\) by \(g\). Each phase strictly increases the residual distance from \(s\) to \(t\), so at most \(|V|-1\) blocking-flow phases occur. A standard current-arc implementation constructs each blocking flow in \(O(|V||E|)\) time, giving total running time \(O(|V|^2|E|)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dinic repeatedly augments by a blocking flow in the residual level graph. At most |V|-1 phases occur, and a standard O(|V||E|)-time blocking-flow implementation gives total running time O(|V|^2|E|).

knowledge_statements.title: Karzanov Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preflow-based construction of blocking flows in an acyclic layered network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L=(V,A)\) be an acyclic residual level network. Initialize zero flow and process internal vertices by forward pushes along admissible outgoing arcs, permitting temporary positive excess. When a vertex can send no further flow, process its remaining excess backward along incoming flow-carrying arcs; delete vertices or arcs that cannot participate further. Continue until every internal vertex is balanced and every directed \(s\)-\(t\) path contains a saturated arc. The resulting feasible flow is blocking in \(L\) and may be used as one phase of a layered maximum-flow method.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Karzanov-style procedures construct a blocking flow by forward preflow pushes, backward excess balancing, and elimination of unusable layered-network elements.
assumptions_latex: \(L=(V,A)\) is a finite acyclic level network.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\) is feasible and every directed \(s\)-\(t\) path in \(L\) contains an arc saturated by \(g\).

knowledge_statements.title: Layered Network Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual level graph used by shortest-augmenting-path blocking-flow methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a feasible flow \(f\), let \(G_f=(V,E_f)\) be its residual network and define \(d(v)=\operatorname{dist}_{G_f}(s,v)\), with \(d(v)=+\infty\) when \(v\) is unreachable. The layered network is \[L_f=\bigl(V,\{(v,w)\in E_f:d(v)<+\infty,\ d(w)=d(v)+1\}\bigr),\] with the residual capacities inherited from \(G_f\). It is acyclic, every directed \(s\)-\(t\) path in it has exactly \(d(t)\) arcs, and these paths are precisely the shortest residual augmenting paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The layered network retains residual arcs advancing one breadth-first level; it is acyclic and contains exactly the shortest residual source–sink paths.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is a feasible flow in a finite directed network.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_f\) is acyclic and its \(s\)-\(t\) paths are exactly the shortest \(s\)-\(t\) paths of \(G_f\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Layered Residual Network
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the level graph induced by exact residual distances to the sink and records its shortest-path structure and optional pruning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a flow \(x\), let \(d(i)\) be the exact distance from node \(i\) to the sink in the residual network \(G(x)\). The layered network contains the residual arcs \((i,j)\) satisfying \(d(i)=d(j)+1\). Consequently, every source--sink path in the layered network is a shortest source--sink path in \(G(x)\). Arcs contained in no such path may be deleted. With \(V_k=\{i:d(i)=k\}\), every retained arc is directed from some \(V_k\) to \(V_{k-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a given flow, compute exact residual distances to the sink and retain residual arcs whose distance decreases by one. Every source–sink path in this layered network is shortest in the residual network. Arcs on no source–sink path may be deleted, and every retained arc goes from layer k to layer k−1.
assumptions_latex: x\text{ is a flow with residual network }G(x).
d(i)\text{ is the exact distance from }i\text{ to the sink in }G(x).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (i,j)\in A_L\iff (i,j)\in A(G(x))\text{ and }d(i)=d(j)+1;\quad \text{every }s\text{--}t\text{ path in }G_L\text{ is shortest in }G(x).

knowledge_statements.title: Blocking-Flow Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Saturated-arc certificate that a layered-network flow is blocking.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g\) be a feasible \(s\)-\(t\) flow in a finite layered network \(L=(V,A)\). Form the subgraph \(H_g\) from arcs having positive residual capacity after routing \(g\). The reachability set \(S=\{v:v\text{ is reachable from }s\text{ in }H_g\}\) is a verifiable blocking-flow certificate when \(t\notin S\): every arc of \(L\) leaving \(S\) is saturated, hence every directed \(s\)-\(t\) path contains a saturated arc. Conversely, if every directed \(s\)-\(t\) path contains a saturated arc, then \(t\notin S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Residual unreachability of the sink certifies that every layered source–sink path contains a saturated arc, so the flow is blocking.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\text{ is blocking}\iff t\notin S\).

vertices reachable from the source in that subgraph

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Forward augmenting paths and maximal layered-network flows
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines layered-network flow maximality and distinguishes it from global maximum-flow optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N=(s,t,V,A,b)\) be a layered network and let \(g\) be a flow in \(N\). An augmenting path with respect to \(g\) is forward if it uses no backward arcs. The flow \(g\) is maximal, not necessarily maximum, if and only if there is no forward augmenting path in \(N\) with respect to \(g\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a layered network, an augmenting path is forward when it uses no backward arc. A flow is maximal, which does not mean maximum, exactly when no forward augmenting path remains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g\text{ is maximal}\iff\nexists\text{ a forward augmenting path in }N\text{ with respect to }g.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bipartite Push–Relabel Operation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Push–relabel operation specialized to two-arc admissible paths in a bipartite residual network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given node \(i\), if an admissible residual arc \((i,j)\) and then an admissible residual arc \((j,k)\) exist, push \(\delta=\min\{e(i),r_{ij},r_{jk}\}\) units along \(i-j-k\). If \((i,j)\) is admissible but no admissible \((j,k)\) exists, replace \(d(j)\) by \(\min\{d(k)+1:(j,k)\in A(j),\ r_{jk}>0\}\). If no admissible \((i,j)\) exists, replace \(d(i)\) by \(\min\{d(j)+1:(i,j)\in A(i),\ r_{ij}>0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting at i, push the maximum permitted amount along an admissible two-arc residual path i-j-k. If the second admissible arc is unavailable, relabel j; if the first is unavailable, relabel i.

e(i)\text{ denotes excess, }r_{uv}\text{ residual capacity, and }d\text{ a distance label}

knowledge_statements.title: Generic Preflow–Push
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic push–relabel algorithm for directed maximum flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize the preflow by saturating arcs leaving \(s\), set \(h(s)=|V|\), and set \(h(v)=0\) for \(v\ne s\). While an active vertex \(v\notin\{s,t\}\) has excess \(e(v)>0\), push \(\delta=\min\{e(v),u_f(v,w)\}\) on any residual arc \((v,w)\) with \(h(v)=h(w)+1\). If no such arc exists, relabel \(v\) by \(h(v)=1+\min\{h(w):(v,w)\in E_f\}\). When no active internal vertex remains, the preflow is a feasible maximum \(s\)-\(t\) flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generic push–relabel repeatedly sends excess along admissible residual arcs and raises blocked vertex labels until the preflow becomes a maximum flow.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite directed capacitated network.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e(v)=0\) for every \(v\notin\{s,t\}\), and the resulting flow is maximum.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational unit for processing a selected active node under the stated generic preflow–push selection convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A node examination of a selected active node \(i\) is the consecutive sequence of push operations from \(i\) continued until either the excess of \(i\) becomes zero or \(i\) is relabeled. knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic preflow-push procedure for maximum s-t flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a network $(G,u,s,t)$ and $n:=|V(G)|$, initialize $f(e):=u(e)$ for every $e\in\delta^+(s)$ and $f(e):=0$ otherwise; set $\psi(s):=n$ and $\psi(v):=0$ for $v\neq s$. The specified output is a maximum source-to-sink flow.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Push and Relabel Operations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines push state updates, saturating and nonsaturating pushes, and relabeling in generic preflow–push.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A push of \(\delta\) units from \(i\) to \(j\) performs \[e(i)\leftarrow e(i)-\delta,\quad r_{ij}\leftarrow r_{ij}-\delta,\quad e(j)\leftarrow e(j)+\delta,\quad r_{ji}\leftarrow r_{ji}+\delta.\] The push is saturating if \(\delta\) equals the forward residual capacity before the update and nonsaturating otherwise. Under the standard choice \(\delta=\min\{e(i),r_{ij}\}\), a nonsaturating push makes \(e(i)=0\). A relabel operation increases \(d(i)\) to create an admissible outgoing residual arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A push transfers excess from one vertex to another while decreasing forward residual capacity and increasing reverse residual capacity. It is saturating when it exhausts the forward residual capacity. With the standard push amount, a nonsaturating push clears the sending vertex's excess. Relabeling increases a distance label to create an admissible arc.

\delta=\min\{e(i),r_{ij}\}\text{ for the conclusion about a nonsaturating push clearing }e(i).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Active Nodes and Valid Push–Relabel Labellings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Activity and distance-label definitions for the generic preflow–push method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a preflow \(x\), a node \(v\in V\setminus\{r,s\}\) is active if and only if \(f_x(v)>0\). Consequently, a preflow is a flow if and only if it has no active nodes. With \(n=|V|\), a vector \(d\in(\mathbb Z_+\cup\{\infty\})^V\) is a valid labelling with respect to \(x\) if \(d(r)=n\), \(d(s)=0\), and \(d(v)\le d(w)+1\) for every arc \(vw\in E(G(x))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An internal node is active exactly when it has positive excess, and a preflow is a flow exactly when it has no active nodes. A valid label gives the source value n and the sink value zero and satisfies the stated one-step inequality on every residual arc.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d\text{ is valid with respect to }x\iff d(r)=n,\ d(s)=0,\ \text{and }d(v)\le d(w)+1\ \forall vw\in E(G(x)).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies the initialization and single-vertex processing procedures for generic preflow–push.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual Digraph, Preflows, and Pushes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Foundational definitions and the push-preservation property for the generic preflow–push maximum-flow method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a directed network with source \(r\), sink \(s\), capacities \(u\), and \(0\le x\le u\), use the convention \(u_{wv}=x_{wv}=0\) when \(vw\in E\) and \(wv\notin E\). The auxiliary digraph \(G(x)\) contains \(vw\) if and only if \(x_{wv}>0\) or \(x_{vw}<u_{vw}\), and its residual capacity is \(\widetilde u_{vw}=u_{vw}-x_{vw}+x_{wv}\). The vector \(x\) is a preflow if \(f_x(v)\ge0\) for every \(v\in V\setminus\{r,s\}\), and it is feasible when also \(0\le x\le u\). If \(\widetilde u_{vw}>0\), \(f_x(v)>0\), and \(0\le\varepsilon\le\min\{\widetilde u_{vw},f_x(v)\}\), pushing \(\varepsilon\) units from \(v\) to \(w\) produces another feasible preflow. If both orientations are original arcs, this push is implemented by decreasing \(x_{wv}\) by \(\varepsilon'=\min\{\varepsilon,x_{wv}\}\) and increasing \(x_{vw}\) by \(\varepsilon-\varepsilon'\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The residual digraph has a forward arc whenever unused forward capacity or cancellable reverse flow exists, with residual capacity equal to their sum. A feasible preflow obeys capacities but permits nonnegative excess at internal nodes. A push bounded by both the residual capacity and the tail's excess preserves feasible-preflow status; antiparallel flow is canceled first.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x'\text{ obtained by the push is a feasible preflow.}

\(\widetilde u_{vw}\) denotes its residual capacity and \(f_x(v)\) the available excess at \(v\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Run generic push–relabel with a FIFO queue \(Q\) initially containing all active internal vertices. Remove the vertex \(v\) at the head and discharge it by valid admissible pushes and relabels until \(e(v)=0\). Whenever a push changes an internal vertex \(w\ne v\) from zero excess to positive excess, append \(w\) to \(Q\) if it is not already present. Continue until \(Q\) is empty. The output is a maximum flow; with standard current-arc bookkeeping, the FIFO variant has worst-case running time \(O(|V|^3)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: FIFO push–relabel fully discharges active vertices in queue order and computes a maximum flow in O(|V|^3) worst-case time.

knowledge_statements.title: Highest-Label Selection Variant
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum-height active-vertex scheduling for generic push–relabel.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Run generic push–relabel while maintaining buckets \(B_i=\{v\notin\{s,t\}:e(v)>0,\ h(v)=i\}\). At each selection step choose a nonempty bucket of maximum index and discharge a vertex \(v\) from it using admissible pushes and relabels. Update bucket membership whenever excess or height changes, and stop when all buckets are empty. Because every selected vertex is active and all push–relabel invariants are preserved, termination yields a feasible maximum \(s\)-\(t\) flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The highest-label variant always discharges an active vertex of maximum height; bucket maintenance makes this selection efficient without changing correctness.
assumptions_latex: Buckets accurately represent active vertices by height.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_i=\varnothing\) for every \(i\), and the resulting flow is maximum.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Potential changes under highest-label preflow-push operations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operation-wise changes in the potential \(\Phi\); the meanings of \(D(i)\), \(K\), and maximal active node are inherited from the associated potential analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a maximal active node \(i\): (a) a nonsaturating push does not increase \(\Phi\), and decreases \(\Phi\) by at least one if \(|D(i)|\le K\); (b) a saturating push can increase \(\Phi\) by at most \(K\); and (c) relabeling \(i\) can increase \(\Phi\) by at most \(K\). Introducing current arcs does not increase \(\Phi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the potential used in the highest-label analysis, a nonsaturating push from a maximal active node never increases the potential and decreases it by at least one when the node's D-set has size at most K. A saturating push or relabel can increase the potential by at most K, while introducing current arcs cannot increase it.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Highest-label preflow-push scheduling and bucket implementation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Highest-label active-node selection, its label-indexed list implementation, and the resulting elementary nonsaturating-push bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At each node examination, select an active node with maximum distance label \(h^*=\max\{d(i):i\text{ is active}\}\). Maintain \(\operatorname{LIST}(k)=\{i:i\text{ is active and }d(i)=k\}\) for \(1\le k\le 2n-1\), and let \(\mathrm{level}\) upper-bound the largest index of a nonempty list. Scanning downward from \(\mathrm{level}\) finds a highest-label active node. If at most \(2n^2\) relabel operations occur, then the algorithm performs \(O(n^3)\) node examinations and therefore \(O(n^3)\) nonsaturating pushes. The total increase of \(\mathrm{level}\) is at most \(2n^2\), and its total decrease is at most \(2n^2+n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Highest-label preflow-push selects an active node with the greatest distance label. Label-indexed lists and a downward-scanned level pointer implement the selection. Given at most 2n² relabels, there are O(n³) node examinations and nonsaturating pushes, and aggregate list scanning is bounded by the movement of the level pointer.
assumptions_latex: \text{The network has }n\text{ nodes and the algorithm maintains valid preflow-push distance labels.}
\text{The algorithm performs at most }2n^2\text{ relabel operations.}
\text{Each node examination entails at most one nonsaturating push.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N_{\mathrm{examinations}}=O(n^3),\qquad N_{\mathrm{nonsat}}=O(n^3),\qquad \Delta^+\mathrm{level}\le 2n^2,\qquad \Delta^-\mathrm{level}\le 2n^2+n.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Highest-Label Push–Relabel Method
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Highest-label specialization of the preflow–push method for static maximum flow, including its valid-label invariant and optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain a preflow \(f\) and \(p:V\to\mathbb Z_+\) satisfying \(p(s)=n\), \(p(t)=0\), and \((u,v)\in A_f\Rightarrow p(v)\ge p(u)-1\). Initialize by saturating arcs leaving \(s\), assigning zero flow elsewhere, setting \(p(s)=n\), and setting all other labels to zero. While active vertices exist, choose an active vertex \(u\) of maximum label. Push \(\min\{r_f(u,v),\operatorname{excess}_f(u)\}\) on an admissible residual arc \((u,v)\) with \(p(v)=p(u)-1\); if none exists, set \(p(u)\leftarrow p(u)+1\). For fixed \(f\), such a labeling exists if and only if \(D_f\) has no \(s\)-\(t\) path. Hence, if \(f\) is an \(s\)-\(t\) flow admitting such a labeling, then \(f\) is maximum.

f\text{ is a preflow, }A_f\text{ is its residual-arc set, and }r_f\text{ denotes residual capacity}.
p:V\to\mathbb Z_+,\quad p(s)=n,\quad p(t)=0,\quad (u,v)\in A_f\Rightarrow p(v)\ge p(u)-1.

knowledge_statements.title: Active-Vertex Scheduling Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correctness invariance and operational effects of active-vertex selection rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a push–relabel execution always selects an active internal vertex, performs only valid pushes and relabels, and continues until no active internal vertex remains. Then the choice among FIFO, highest-label, or any other eligible scheduling rule does not alter correctness: the terminal preflow is a maximum flow. Scheduling can nevertheless alter the order and number of nonsaturating pushes, relabels, scans, and queue or bucket operations, so two rules may have different worst-case bounds and practical performance on the same network family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any valid active-vertex schedule preserves push–relabel correctness, but schedules differ in operation counts, data-structure costs, worst-case bounds, and practical behavior.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: List-based discharge implementation of push–relabel.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize a list \(L\) of all vertices in \(V\setminus\{s,t\}\), initialize the standard preflow and valid heights, and scan \(L\) from the front. knowledge_statements.title: Global-Relabel Heuristic
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact residual-distance reset used during push–relabel execution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At selected times during push–relabel, run a reverse breadth-first search from \(t\) in the current residual network. Reset \(h(v)=\operatorname{dist}_{G_f}(v,t)\) for every vertex that can reach \(t\), set \(h(v)=|V|\) for other vertices, and retain \(h(s)=|V|\). Resume ordinary push and relabel operations. The reset labels satisfy \(h(v)\le h(w)+1\) on every residual arc \((v,w)\), preserve the preflow, and therefore preserve correctness while supplying sharper distance information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Global relabeling recomputes exact residual distances to the sink by reverse breadth-first search, preserving correctness and improving height information.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h(v)\le h(w)+1\) for every residual arc \((v,w)\), and the preflow is unchanged.

children.title: Gap Heuristic
children.top_down_role: Use of missing label levels to identify vertices separated from the sink.

knowledge_statements.title: Gap Heuristic
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Label update for a push–relabel maximum-flow implementation after an empty height level is detected.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G_f=(V,E_f)\) be the residual network, let \(t\) be the sink, and let \(h:V\to\{0,\ldots,2n-1\}\) be a valid height labeling with \(h(t)=0\), where \(n=|V|\). If some level \(k<n\) is empty and \(U=\{v\in V:k<h(v)<n\}\), replace \(h(v)\) by \(n+1\) for every \(v\in U\). Each vertex in \(U\) has no residual path to \(t\), so it need not be processed toward the sink at its former height. Continue ordinary admissible pushes and relabels, excluding \(s\) and \(t\) from the active-vertex queue.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When a height level is empty, vertices above that gap but below the source height cannot reach the sink and are moved to a permanently high level.
assumptions_latex: \(G_f\) is the residual network of a feasible preflow.
\(h(u)\le h(v)+1\) for every residual arc \((u,v)\in E_f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\in U\Longrightarrow t\text{ is unreachable from }v\text{ in }G_f\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The gap implication is standard, but no source or inspectable locator supports the precise update rule. The plain statement should also say that affected labels remain at least n, rather than calling n+1 a permanently fixed level.

knowledge_statements.title: Combined Heuristic Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic composition of global relabeling and gap relabeling within push–relabel.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a residual network \(G_f\), initialize heights by a reverse breadth-first search from \(t\), assigning each vertex its residual distance to \(t\) and assigning unreachable vertices height at least \(n\). Perform admissible pushes and local relabels. After every prescribed budget \(T\ge1\) of elementary operations, or when another fixed trigger fires, recompute all heights by reverse breadth-first search. Between recomputations, whenever a level \(k<n\) becomes empty, apply the gap update to every vertex whose height lies strictly between \(k\) and \(n\). Stop when no active vertex other than \(s\) or \(t\) remains; output the resulting feasible maximum flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regime periodically rebuilds exact sink-distance labels and applies gap updates between rebuilds, while retaining the ordinary push–relabel stopping rule.
assumptions_latex: \(G_f\) is maintained from a feasible preflow.
\(T\) and every additional global-relabel trigger are fixed before execution.
Local push and relabel operations preserve valid height labels.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{termination with no internal active vertex implies that the induced feasible flow is maximum}\).

notation.meaning: operation budget between scheduled global relabels

knowledge_statements.title: Directed Source–Sink Minimum Cuts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directed capacitated source–sink cuts and their equality in value with maximum source–sink flows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph with capacities \(c:A	o\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\) and distinct vertices \(s,t\in V\). For \(S\subseteq V\), define \(\delta^+(S)=\{(u,v)\in A:u\in S,\ v
otin S\}\). An \(s\)-\(t\) cut is a set \(S\) with \(s\in S\) and \(t
otin S\), and its capacity is \(c(\delta^+(S))=\sum_{a\in\delta^+(S)}c(a)\). If \(\lambda(s,t)=\min\{c(\delta^+(S)):s\in S,\ t
otin S\}\), then \(\lambda(s,t)\) equals the maximum value of a feasible \(s\)-\(t\) flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directed source–sink minimum cut minimizes the capacity of arcs leaving a set containing the source and excluding the sink, and its value equals the maximum feasible source–sink flow value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda(s,t)=\max\{|f|:f\text{ is a feasible }s\text{-}t\text{ flow}\}\).

notation.meaning: arcs directed from the set to its complement

knowledge_statements.title: Undirected Global Minimum Cut
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum nontrivial cut in a finite undirected capacitated graph, without designated terminals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph with \(|V|\ge2\) and capacities \(c:E\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\). For a nonempty proper set \(S\subset V\), let \(\delta(S)=\{uv\in E:|\{u,v\}\cap S|=1\}\) and \(c(\delta(S))=\sum_{e\in\delta(S)}c(e)\). An undirected global minimum cut is any bipartition \(\{S,V\setminus S\}\) attaining \(\lambda(G)=\min_{\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V}c(\delta(S))\). Because \(\delta(S)=\delta(V\setminus S)\), complementary shores define the same cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A global minimum cut is a nontrivial vertex bipartition whose crossing undirected edges have minimum total capacity among all bipartitions.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph with \(|V|\ge2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda(G)=\min_{\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V}\sum_{e\in\delta(S)}c(e)\).

notation.meaning: undirected edge boundary of a vertex set

knowledge_statements.title: Gomory–Hu Cut Trees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: All-pairs minimum-cut values represented by one weighted tree for an undirected capacitated graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every finite undirected capacitated graph \(G=(V,E,c)\), there exists a weighted tree \(T=(V,F,w)\) such that, for every distinct \(s,t\in V\), the minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut value in \(G\) equals \(\min\{w(e):e\text{ lies on the unique }s\text{-}t\text{ path in }T\}\). Moreover, deleting any minimum-weight edge on that tree path partitions \(V\) into two shores that form a minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut in \(G\). Thus one tree stores all pairwise minimum-cut values and supplies a corresponding cut for every terminal pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Gomory–Hu tree stores every pairwise minimum-cut value as the lightest edge on the corresponding tree path and recovers an attaining cut.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_G(s,t)=\min_{e\in P_T(s,t)}w(e)\) for all distinct \(s,t\in V\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Realizability criterion for a symmetric flow matrix
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes symmetric matrices realizable as network flow matrices using only the hypotheses stated in the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A symmetric matrix \(V=(v_{ij})\) is the flow matrix of some network if and only if, for all indices \(i,j,k\), \[v_{ij}\geq\min\{v_{ik},v_{kj}\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric matrix is realizable as a network flow matrix exactly when every entry v_ij is at least the minimum of v_ik and v_kj for every triple of indices.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Cut Cactus Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cactus encoding of every global minimum cut of a finite undirected capacitated graph with positive global minimum-cut value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E,c)\) be a finite undirected capacitated graph with \(|V|\ge2\) and positive global minimum-cut value \(\lambda(G)>0\). There exist a cactus graph \(C\) and a map \(\phi:V\to V(C)\) such that every global minimum cut of \(G\) is the inverse image under \(\phi\) of a bipartition obtained either by deleting one bridge of \(C\) or by deleting two edges belonging to one cycle of \(C\). Conversely, every such bridge deletion or same-cycle edge-pair deletion induces a global minimum cut of \(G\). Every edge of \(C\) belongs to at most one simple cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the global minimum-cut value is positive, a cactus represents all global minimum cuts by bridge deletions or by deleting two edges from one cactus cycle, and every represented deletion induces a global minimum cut.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{M}(G)=\{\phi^{-1}(X):X\text{ is a shore induced by a bridge deletion or a same-cycle edge-pair deletion in }C\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Cut Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sparse subgraph certificate preserving every undirected cut up to a prescribed threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be an undirected multigraph with \(n=|V|\), and let \(k\) be a positive integer. A sparse \(k\)-cut certificate is a spanning subgraph \(H=(V,F)\) satisfying \(|F|\le k(n-1)\) and, for every \(S\subseteq V\), \(\min\{k,|\delta_H(S)|\}=\min\{k,|\delta_G(S)|\}\). Consequently, every cut of size less than \(k\) is preserved exactly, while every cut having at least \(k\) edges retains at least \(k\) certificate edges. Such a certificate is sufficient to verify all cut queries below threshold \(k\) using only \(O(kn)\) edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sparse certificate uses at most k(n−1) edges, preserves every cut smaller than k exactly, and keeps at least k edges in every larger cut.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|F|\le k(n-1)\quad\text{and}\quad\min\{k,|\delta_H(S)|\}=\min\{k,|\delta_G(S)|\}\text{ for all }S\subseteq V\).

children.title: Integral-Capacity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Maximum-flow settings with integer-valued capacities.

knowledge_statements.title: Integral-Capacity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integrality and pseudo-polynomial augmentation bound for maximum flow with integer capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) have nonnegative integral capacities, let \(m=|A|\), and define \(U_s=\sum_{a\in\delta^+(s)}c(a)\). Starting from the zero flow, Ford–Fulkerson augmentation along any residual \(s\)-\(t\) path preserves integrality and increases the flow value by at least one. Hence it terminates after at most \(F^*\le U_s\) augmentations, where \(F^*\) is the maximum-flow value. If a residual path is found in \(O(m)\) time, the resulting bound is \(O(mF^*)\subseteq O(mU_s)\). The dependence on numerical capacity magnitude makes this bound pseudo-polynomial rather than polynomial in binary input length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integer capacities yield an integral maximum flow and at most F* unit-or-larger augmentations, giving an O(mF*) pseudo-polynomial Ford–Fulkerson bound.
assumptions_latex: Each augmentation uses a residual source–sink path and its bottleneck capacity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{aug}}\le F^*\le U_s\quad\text{and}\quad T=O(mF^*)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Rational-Capacity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction of rational-capacity maximum flow to an integer-capacity instance by common-denominator scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let every arc capacity \(c(a)\) be a nonnegative rational number. Choose a positive integer \(D\) such that \(Dc(a)\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}\) for all arcs, and define \(c'(a)=Dc(a)\). A flow \(f\) is feasible for \(c\) if and only if \(Df\) is feasible for \(c'\), and optimal values satisfy \(F'^*=DF^*\). Therefore integral-capacity termination arguments apply after scaling. However, \(D\) and the scaled capacities may be exponentially large relative to their binary encodings, so the augmentation bound inherited from integer scaling is not a polynomial-time bound in the original input length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Common-denominator scaling turns rational capacities into integers and preserves optimal flows, but the scaled magnitudes may make augmentation bounds only pseudo-polynomial.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is optimal for }c\Longleftrightarrow Df\text{ is optimal for }Dc\), with \(F'^*=DF^*\).

children.title: Real-Capacity Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Real-Capacity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence and duality remain valid over real capacities, but arbitrary-path augmentation need not terminate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite network with capacities \(c:A\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\), the feasible-flow polytope is compact and a maximum flow exists; its value equals the minimum directed \(s\)-\(t\) cut capacity. Nevertheless, the arbitrary-path Ford–Fulkerson rule has no discrete lower bound on positive augmentations. There exist finite networks with irrational capacities and admissible sequences of augmenting paths for which infinitely many augmentations occur and no finite iterate is a maximum flow. Thus max-flow existence and duality do not imply finite termination of an unrestricted augmenting-path selection rule over arbitrary real capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximum flows and minimum cuts remain well defined for real capacities, but arbitrary Ford–Fulkerson path choices can produce infinitely many augmentations with irrational data.
assumptions_latex: Ford–Fulkerson may choose any residual source–sink path.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_f|f|=\min_S c(\delta^+(S))\), but finite termination is not guaranteed for arbitrary augmenting-path choices.

notation.meaning: arcs leaving a source-side cut shore

children.title: Capacity-Domain Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Algorithmic and representational distinctions across capacity domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Capacity-Domain Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete augmentation bounds require positive capacity granularity; max-flow duality itself does not.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose every positive residual bottleneck encountered by an augmenting-path method is at least \(\Delta>0\). If the maximum-flow value is \(F^*\), each augmentation increases the value by at least \(\Delta\), so at most \(\lceil F^*/\Delta\rceil\) augmentations occur. Integral capacities provide \(\Delta=1\), and rational capacities provide such a \(\Delta\) after common-denominator scaling. For unrestricted real capacities, no input-independent positive granularity need exist, so this counting argument fails even though maximum-flow minimum-cut duality remains valid. Algorithms whose operation bounds do not depend on capacity magnitudes avoid this domain boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Augmentation counting works when positive bottlenecks have fixed granularity; arbitrary real capacities remove that guarantee without invalidating max-flow minimum-cut duality.
assumptions_latex: Every augmentation increases the flow by its positive residual bottleneck.
A common lower bound \(\Delta>0\) exists when the counting bound is invoked.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{aug}}\le\lceil F^*/\Delta\rceil\); without such \(\Delta\), this bound is unavailable.

notation.meaning: lower bound on positive augmentation amounts

Then the maximum value of a feasible \(s\)-\(t\) flow equals the maximum cardinality of a family of pairwise arc-disjoint directed \(s\)-\(t\) paths.

knowledge_statements.title: Small-Capacity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction of capacity-dependent bounds when integral capacities are polynomially bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a maximum-flow instance have integral capacities and let \(U=\max_{e\in E}u_e\). If \(U\le n^k\) for a fixed constant \(k\), then \(\log(U+1)=O(\log n)\). Consequently, any bound polynomial in \(n\), \(m\), and \(\log(U+1)\) is polynomial in the graph dimensions. Moreover, a pseudopolynomial bound of the form \(O(U\,p(n,m))\), where \(p\) is a polynomial, becomes polynomial in \(n\) and \(m\) under this small-capacity assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomially bounded integral capacities turn logarithmic capacity dependence, and even linear pseudopolynomial dependence on the largest capacity, into graph-dimension polynomial bounds.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a directed network with \(n=|V|\) and \(m=|E|\).
\(u_e\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) and \(U\le n^k\) for a fixed \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\log(U+1)=O(\log n)\), and \(O(U\,p(n,m))\) is polynomial in \(n,m\).

notation.meaning: an arbitrary polynomial in graph dimensions

children.title: Capacity-Range Sensitivity

knowledge_statements.title: Capacity-Range Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependence of maximum-flow running times on the numerical capacity range.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For integral capacities, set \(U=\max_{e\in E}u_e\). Under uniform scaling \(u'_e=\lambda u_e\) by an integer \(\lambda\ge1\), the graph dimensions remain \(n,m\), while \(U'=\lambda U\). Thus a weakly polynomial factor \(\log(U+1)\) changes to \(\log(\lambda U+1)\), a pseudopolynomial factor \(U\) changes to \(\lambda U\), and a strongly polynomial operation bound depending only on \(n,m\) is unchanged. Capacity scaling therefore distinguishes logarithmic, magnitude, and magnitude-independent complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaling capacities affects logarithmic dependence mildly, pseudopolynomial dependence proportionally, and strongly polynomial operation bounds not at all.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U'=\lambda U\), separating logarithmic, pseudopolynomial, and strongly polynomial sensitivity.

knowledge_statements.title: Dense Graph Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic density convention for simple directed maximum-flow networks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A family \((G_n)\) of simple directed networks is in the dense-graph regime when \(G_n=(V_n,E_n)\), \(|V_n|=n\), and \(|E_n|=m_n=\Theta(n^2)\). Equivalently, there exist constants \(c,C>0\) and \(n_0\) such that \(c n^2\le m_n\le C n^2\) for all \(n\ge n_0\). In this regime, a running-time bound expressed in \(m\) is evaluated after the substitution \(m=\Theta(n^2)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A simple directed graph family is dense when its number of arcs grows quadratically with its number of vertices.
assumptions_latex: \((G_n)\) is a family of simple directed graphs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m_n=\Theta(n^2)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Graph Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-size sparsity convention for directed maximum-flow networks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A family \((G_n)\) of directed networks is in the sparse-graph regime when \(G_n=(V_n,E_n)\), \(|V_n|=n\), and \(|E_n|=m_n=O(n)\). children.title: Density-Sensitive Complexity Crossover
children.top_down_role: Instance-density thresholds that change the preferred complexity bound or implementation family.

knowledge_statements.title: Density-Sensitive Complexity Crossover
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic crossover between edge-sensitive and vertex-sensitive maximum-flow bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose two maximum-flow algorithms have worst-case bounds \(T_A(n,m)=O(m\alpha(n))\) and \(T_B(n,m)=O(n^2\beta(n))\), where \(\alpha,\beta>0\). Their asymptotic crossover occurs at \(m=\Theta(n^2\beta(n)/\alpha(n))\). Algorithm \(A\) has the smaller displayed bound when \(m=o(n^2\beta(n)/\alpha(n))\), while algorithm \(B\) has the smaller displayed bound when \(m=\omega(n^2\beta(n)/\alpha(n))\). Thus sparsity can change which complexity guarantee is preferable even for the same problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equating an edge-sensitive bound with a vertex-sensitive bound identifies the graph density at which their asymptotic ranking reverses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The crossover density is \(m=\Theta(n^2\beta(n)/\alpha(n))\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: crossover follows by equating the two stated asymptotic bounds
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

children.title: Weakly Polynomial Maximum Flow

knowledge_statements.title: Weakly Polynomial Maximum Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bit-complexity definition for integral-capacity maximum flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a directed maximum-flow instance with integral capacities \(0\le u_e\le U\), an algorithm is weakly polynomial if its running time is bounded by a polynomial in the binary input length. With explicit arc encoding, this permits a bound polynomial in \(n\), \(m\), and \(\log(U+1)\). Hence the bound may depend on the number of bits used to encode the capacities, but not polynomially on their magnitudes merely because they are written in binary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weakly polynomial maximum-flow algorithm runs polynomially in graph size and capacity encoding length, so its bound may contain logarithmic numeric dependence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The running time is \(\operatorname{poly}(n,m,\log(U+1))\).

knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Polynomial Maximum Flow

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A maximum-flow algorithm is strongly polynomial if the number of arithmetic operations and comparisons is bounded by a polynomial in \(n=|V|\) and \(m=|E|\), independently of the numerical values and encoding lengths of the capacities, and every intermediate number has encoding length polynomial in the input length. Arithmetic operations and comparisons use the standard exact-arithmetic model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The operation count is \(\operatorname{poly}(n,m)\), independent of capacity magnitudes, with polynomially bounded intermediate encoding lengths.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For integral-capacity maximum flow, let \(U=\max_{e\in E}u_e\), with capacities encoded in binary. A running-time guarantee polynomial in \(U\), even when its remaining dependence is polynomial in the graph dimensions, is generally pseudopolynomial because \(U\) requires only \(\Theta(\log(U+1))\) bits to encode. A guarantee polynomial in the full binary input length, and hence possibly polynomial in \(n\), \(m\), and \(\log(U+1)\), is weakly polynomial. Strong polynomiality additionally requires an arithmetic-operation bound polynomial only in \(n\) and \(m\), independent of capacity values and encoding lengths, together with polynomially bounded intermediate encoding lengths. Strongly polynomial algorithms are also weakly polynomial, so these labels describe increasingly restrictive guarantees rather than three disjoint algorithm classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial dependence on capacity magnitude is generally pseudopolynomial; polynomial dependence on binary encoding length is weakly polynomial; and a graph-dimension-only operation bound with controlled intermediate encodings is strongly polynomial. Strong polynomiality is a stricter form of weak polynomiality.
knowledge_statements.title: Numeric-Dependence Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a finite directed graph \(G=(V,E)\), arc costs \(c_e\in\mathbb R\), and bounds \(\ell_e,u_e\in\mathbb R\) with \(\ell_e\le u_e\), assume that the bounded-circulation feasible set is nonempty. A minimum-cost circulation is a vector \(x\in\mathbb R^E\) solving
\[\min_{x\in\mathbb R^E}\ \sum_{e\in E}c_e x_e\]
subject to \(\ell_e\le x_e\le u_e\) for every \(e\in E\) and
\[\sum_{e\in\delta^-(v)}x_e-\sum_{e\in\delta^+(v)}x_e=0\qquad(v\in V).\]
Thus every vertex has zero net imbalance, and the objective selects a least-cost feasible circulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assuming a bounded circulation exists, a minimum-cost circulation obeys its arc bounds and flow conservation at every vertex while minimizing total linear arc cost.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a finite directed network \(G=(V,E)\) with distinct source \(s\in V\) and sink \(t\in V\), arc costs \(c_e\in\mathbb R\), capacities \(u_e\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\), and a prescribed value \(q\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\), assume that a feasible flow of value \(q\) exists. A minimum-cost source-sink flow is a vector \(x\in\mathbb R^E\) minimizing \(\sum_{e\in E}c_e x_e\) subject to \(0\le x_e\le u_e\) for every \(e\in E\),
\[\sum_{e\in\delta^-(v)}x_e-\sum_{e\in\delta^+(v)}x_e=0\qquad(v\in V\setminus\{s,t\}),\]
and
\[\sum_{e\in\delta^+(s)}x_e-\sum_{e\in\delta^-(s)}x_e=q,
\qquad
\sum_{e\in\delta^-(t)}x_e-\sum_{e\in\delta^+(t)}x_e=q.\]
The value \(q\) is fixed rather than optimized.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Among feasible flows carrying a prescribed amount from source to sink, a minimum-cost source-sink flow has minimum total arc cost.
knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Cost Source–Sink Flow

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Cost Maximum Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lexicographic optimization of source–sink value followed by flow cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a capacitated directed network with source \(s\), sink \(t\), and arc costs \(c_e\), let \(F^*\) be the maximum feasible \(s\)-to-\(t\) flow value. A minimum-cost maximum flow is any feasible flow \(x\) satisfying \(\operatorname{val}(x)=F^*\) and
\[\sum_{e\in E}c_e x_e=
\min\left\{\sum_{e\in E}c_e y_e: y\text{ is feasible and }\operatorname{val}(y)=F^*\right\}.\]
Thus flow value is optimized first, and cost is minimized only among maximum-value flows.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: First maximize source–sink flow value; then, among all maximum flows, select one of minimum total cost.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and directed with distinct source and sink.
Each arc has a finite nonnegative capacity and a real cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) lexicographically maximizes \((\operatorname{val}(x),-\sum_e c_e x_e)\).

children.title: Lower-Bound Elimination
children.top_down_role: Demand shifts and residual feasibility effects created when positive lower bounds are removed.

knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Bound Elimination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine elimination of arcwise lower bounds in a finite minimum-cost transshipment problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\), let every arc \(a\) have bounds \(\ell_a\le u_a\), and impose \(\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}x_a-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}x_a=b_v\). Define \(y_a=x_a-\ell_a\). Then \(\ell_a\le x_a\le u_a\) is equivalent to \(0\le y_a\le u_a-\ell_a\), while the balance becomes \(\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}y_a-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}y_a=b'_v\), where \(b'_v=b_v-\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}\ell_a+\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}\ell_a\). For linear costs, \(\sum_a c_ax_a=\sum_a c_ay_a+\sum_a c_a\ell_a\), so feasible solutions correspond bijectively and minimizers are preserved.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtract each arc’s lower bound, reduce its capacity accordingly, adjust node supplies, and add the resulting constant to the objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\mapsto y=x-\ell\) is a feasibility-preserving bijection and preserves optimal solutions after an objective constant shift.

knowledge_statements.title: Capacity Normalization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalization of residual arc intervals after lower-bound elimination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each arc \(a\), define its normalized capacity by \(U_a=u_a-\ell_a\) and its normalized flow by \(y_a=x_a-\ell_a\). Then the original interval \([\ell_a,u_a]\) is translated bijectively onto \([0,U_a]\). If \(u_a=+\infty\), use \(U_a=+\infty\); otherwise \(U_a\ge0\) is finite. Thus every bounded minimum-cost flow instance can be written with zero lower bounds and constraints \(0\le y_a\le U_a\), without scaling costs or changing the residual amount of flow permitted on any arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Translate each feasible arc interval to start at zero; its normalized capacity is the original upper bound minus the lower bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \([\ell_a,u_a]\ni x_a\longleftrightarrow y_a=x_a-\ell_a\in[0,u_a-\ell_a]\) is a bijection.

notation.meaning: Normalized upper capacity of arc a.

knowledge_statements.title: Coupled Bound Transformation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous transformation of bounds, balances, and linear cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the program minimizing \(c^{\mathsf T}x\) subject to \(Bx=b\) and \(\ell\le x\le u\), where the node–arc incidence matrix uses \(+1\) at an arc's tail and \(-1\) at its head. With \(x=\ell+y\), the transformed program is \(\min c^{\mathsf T}y+c^{\mathsf T}\ell\) subject to \(By=b-B\ell\) and \(0\le y\le u-\ell\). Consequently, feasibility, differences between objective values, and the ordering of feasible solutions are preserved under the affine correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The same affine substitution must update capacities, node balances, and the objective constant together to produce an equivalent flow problem.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is the incidence matrix of a finite directed graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\mapsto y=x-\ell\) bijects the two feasible sets and preserves their argmin sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Bound-Transformation Feasibility Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact cut criterion for feasibility of lower- and upper-bounded transshipment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be finite, require \(\ell\le x\le u\), and use balances \(Bx=b\) with tail-positive incidence matrix \(B\). A feasible flow exists if and only if \(b(V)=0\) and, for every \(S\subseteq V\), \[\ell(\delta^+(S))-u(\delta^-(S))\le b(S)\le u(\delta^+(S))-\ell(\delta^-(S)).\] Equivalently, after setting \(y=x-\ell\), the zero-lower-bound instance \(By=b-B\ell\), \(0\le y\le u-\ell\), is feasible. Violation of any displayed cut inequality certifies infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The transformed instance is feasible exactly when total supply is zero and every node cut can carry its required net supply within the arc bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stated family of cut inequalities is necessary and sufficient for bounded-flow feasibility.

notation.meaning: Sum of supplies over nodes in S.
Sum of an arc vector q over an arc set F.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two-sided cut criterion is a nontrivial necessary-and-sufficient bounded-flow feasibility theorem. Its signs are consistent with the tail-positive incidence convention, but no source or locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Transshipment-to-Circulation Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction of balanced transshipment to circulation using one auxiliary node and fixed-flow arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) have balances \(Bx=b\), where \(b(V)=0\) and positive \(b_v\) denotes supply. Add a node \(r\). For every \(v\) with \(b_v>0\), add an arc \((r,v)\) having lower and upper bound \(b_v\); for every \(v\) with \(b_v<0\), add an arc \((v,r)\) having both bounds \(-b_v\). Give all new arcs zero cost. Then a flow on the original arcs satisfies \(Bx=b\) exactly when its unique extension using these fixed auxiliary flows is a circulation. Original costs and capacities are unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Attach fixed zero-cost arcs to a new node so that each supply or demand becomes ordinary flow conservation in an augmented circulation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasible transshipments correspond bijectively to feasible circulations in the augmented network, with equal costs.
